"WHEN I WAS A BOY." When I was a boy," the grandsire said To the bright lad by his knee, "Of the victors crowned with fame I read Who triumphed on land and sea! And through the years, from the deathless page, A summons has sounded long: To youth, and manhood, and hoary age, The message is this— Be Strong! ' "When I was a boy—" he paused and said, , To the listener by his knee, "Of the men who were as lights I read In a dark world's history! :hey prized the truth, and were loved f God, And no fear of man they knew; And still, from the glorious heights they trod, The message is this—' Be True " The Quiver, February.

GO A-FISHING. The tide is heavy with the draught, • And fishermen are few! My heart and hands are strong for work, Oh, let me come with you; The land-life that I used to love Has lost its charm for me, And all my light and all my joy Are out upon the sea. My childhood's visions have outlived The dreams of after youth, And, with a soul-enchanting power, Have won me back to truth; Then why must I be land-botiad still, When all that now I crave Is work upon God's wondrous deep, And, in that deep. a grave? Farewell to home, the home I love Lies out beyond the sea; Farewell to wealth, my fisher's coat • Is dower enough for me. Give me my net, a loving heart That spreads both deep and wide, !: Then let me leave all else behind And launch out on the tide.

For multitudes of living hearts Within that ocean move. And all that they are waiting for Are fishing nets of love, That they may breathe the upper air, And see the glory shed • By Mercy's moonbeams shining through The midnight overhead. Why must I wait, and sicken here With unfulfilled desire? Some kindling light I never sought Bath set my soul on fire ! And in that light all things have grown As darkness unto me And through the darkness comes a. voice, "Go, work upon the sea." --Sanday .Atagazine. GIOPEVIEVE IRONS.

.. 'I 1.11 A 1 set Tarittito. • It is not sufficient not to intend to do wrong; we mist Intend to do right, and carry out our intentions also. Not to think is in such a case a crime. A country gentleman, going his rounds one evening, saw a great snake coiled up on his garden walk. He im- mediately got an axe, cut the creature into a hundred pieces, returned to his house, told everybody about his exploit, and went to bed. Next morning his gardener came in great tribulation to complain that some scour,' drel had been in the night and cut to pieces his best gar- den hose. Two persons were once disputing so loudly on the sub- ject of religion that they awoke a big dog which had been sleeping on the hearth before them, and be forth- with barked most furiously. An old divine present, who had been quietly sipping his tea while the disputants were talking and wrangling so boisterously, gave the dog a kick and exclaimed, "Hold your tongue, you silly brute. You know no more about it than they do." "Here is a book mentioned in this paper entitled "Hints on Husbandry," said Miss Smiggle. "I think Ell go down town and buy me a copy." Her brother, to whom the remark was addressed, smiled and said nothing. That evening at the supper-table he inquired, "Did you get the book you spoke of to-day, Miranda?" " Ye-es," was the somewhat reluctant reply. And how did you enjoy it?" "Well, I reckon it's a good enough book, but the title is kind o' disappointin'." She was not very young, but she had money. "Dearest," he began, but she stopped him.— "I antici- pate what you are about to say, Mr. Sampson," she said, "and I would spare your feelings, for it can never, never be. I esteem you highly, and will be a sister to—" "I have four sisters already," he replied bitterly, "four grown sisters, and life is a hideous burden. But oh! Clara," he went op passionately, "if you cannot be my wife, will you not give me a motherbs protecting love? I am an orphan." HEALTH OF BODY AND HEALTH OF MlED.—Health, strength, and ability of body make usually health, strength and ability of brain; and if I were told to pick out the cleverest men in any crowd, I should pick out at once not the tallest, but the strongest and best-made men in it, and say, " There—l may have made a few mis- takes; I may have left out a weakly genius or two; and I may have taken in a huge fool or two. But on the whole, there are the men whose wits I will warrant to do the best work."—The late Cuestas KINGSLZY, in- "Good Words" for February. THE FrasT DERBY.—The Derby stakes were first in- stituted in the year 1780, the Oaks being the elder race by one year. The Earl of Derby of that day—the father of Lady Charlotte Stanley, who married General Bur- goyne—was a sportsman of the old-fashioned thorough- going sort, and for mans' years had a hunting-box for his stag-hounds near to Epsom, called the Oaks; hence the names of these now celebrated races. The picture of his huntsman, Jonathan Griffin, on his grey horse Spanker, may still be seen on the parlour walls of many a snug roadside inn in Surrey. In gratitude for the sport shown to him by his neighbours, in 1779 was first run at Epsom "The Oaks Stakes, for three-year-old fillies." This was won by Lord Derby; and in the next year was wou the first, Derby stakes, for three-year-old eOlt3. From that time to this there has been an unin- terrupted succession of these annual races. Like the St. Leger at Doncaster, these races did not attract any great attention for some years. Here is the full account of the first Derby. Alderman WEBSTER said there was only one feeling in 1 that Council as to the sad circumstances that had rendered that resignation necesstry. (Hear, hear.) He was sure they all agreed is the expression conveying their deepest 1 sympathy and condolence to Mrs. Mackie in the circum- stances that were overwhelming her 3t this moment. (Hear,ll hear.) The DFFVFY MAYOR stid it seemed very sad indeed to think that an intellect so keen and bright as the Mayor's, I matured as it was by the enlarged experienced of many 1 years of steady labour and perseverance and successful ert• i lerprise, and having arrived at the very goal of his very i laudable aspiration to serve the town of his adoption as its ' Mayor and chief magistrate should at that very moment be stricken down in so cruel a manner; and at the very mo- ment, it might also be observed, when his exertions might i have been turned to most profitable account for the town during Her Majesty's Jubilee. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Davies said the Council was placed in an ex- traordinary position that night, having no precedent of such a thing. He then referred to the admirable document which had been dictated by the Mayor, saying that it showed that he must have possessed great strength of mind when he drew it up, and asked whether they could not. adopt any other course than the Immediate acceptance of the resignation. After a short explanation by the Deputy Mayor it was, ho vever, decided unanimously to accept the Mayor's resig- nation. Alderman HOLMES then formally moved "That the Council do hereby declare the office of Mayor of the borough lately held by Dr. Mackie to be vacant by reason of his resignation." Alderman CRAS•DLEY seconded this proposal, which was agreed to. , THE DEATH OF COUNCILLOR BROADBENT. The DEPUTY MAYOR said they had no doubt heard of the melancholy death of Mr. Councillor Broadbent. It was a custom they had adapted to move a vote of condolence with the family of a deceased member, and for that purpose he now begged to move "That this Council receives with deep regrrt the announcement of the death of Charles Broad- bent, Egg , a couocillor of this borough, which took place on the 29th January, and desires to record the loss which the Council has sustained by his death, and to express its appreciation of the valuable services rendered by him to the borough during the period of upwards of 27 years; and that the Town Clerk he requested to convey to the family of the late Mr. Broadbent this expression of the sincere sympathy and condolence of the Council with them on their sad be- reavement " (Hear, hear.) 4" Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the proposal. It was such a painful subject that he felt a diffidence in approaching it; for they did all feel so very keenly their loss that words seemed almost paralysed. He had no doubt that expression would be given by other members of the Corporation of the high esteem in which Mr. Broadbent had been held by that Council. It seemed very sad indeed that in the midst of such a very useful life he should have been removed. They should miss one of the most genial of men; a man of indis- putable ability, a man of most cultured taste, and one with whom an acquaintance was is 'met refined pleasure. (Hear, bear.) He for one felt extremely the loss of Mr. Broad- bent, and he was certain they should have very great diffi. culty in replacing him in that Council. He felt sure that he was expressingnot only his own feeliegs, hut the teet- ings of every member of that Corporation, when he said that they heard with nnmitlgated grief of the loss they had sustained. (Hear, hear.) . Councillor PLATT said he could not allow that occasion to pass without one word of his appreciation of the charac- ter of Mr, Broadbent, Having been Mr. Breadbent's col- league in the representation of the North-eastward, now en- tering the 10th year in succession, Ile felt very deeply his , loss. Last November they were returned together for the fourth time for the term of three years, and then they little thought that in so short a time after that he would begone. (Hear, hear.) He was sure he was expressing the opinion of the whole of the Council when he said Mr. Broadbent not only had their esteem, but also bad their affection. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CROSFIELD said he should like to add his testi- mony to Mr. Broadbent's character. He had known Mr. Broadbent for five and thirty years. and he never heard him tither publicly or privately say a hard word against any- body. He thought the loss of Mr. Broadbent was very great to them, and greater to his family. (Hear, hear.)

The weights, orignally fist. for colts, and 7st. nib. for fillies, were shortly after raised to Bst 71b. and Bst. 21b. respectively, and the distance increased th a mile and a half. With the exception of an alteration in the course in 1848, no change occurred for fifty years. The weights in 1862 were again raised to Bst. 101 b. for colts, and Bst. 71b. for fillies, but the entrance and forfeits have always been the same, and no added money has been ever given."—From Cassell's Greater London for January. A FATAL Poirramr.—The portrait was painted in Brussels, where the diake was in residence, and the last sitting was given on the 4th of June, 1568. His sallow face a mask for the treachery in his mind, thus he looked that day when he signed the secret order of execution for the brilliant conqueror of St. Quentin, the darling of the citizens of Brussels, and for honest bluff Admiral Hoorn, that day when he silenced the kneeling Bishop of Ypres, summoned to shrive the condemned and not to plead for them. Those glittering eyes rested upon the painter putting finishing touches to his portrait, and upon Egmont's trembling countess. Unwilling ears surprised the secret the countess begged for in vain. Keij, the painter, was at his work, and a few words overheard betrayed the impending fate of the two noblemen. Stricken with horror— some say with the very sight of Alva's face at the moment—weighed down by the burden of a State secret which the whole country was trembling to divine, Keij went home. Whilst the Countess Egmont and her twelve children nursed false hopes in their convent, the sensitive soul of the artist sickened of this crowning ad- dition to the despair and the horrors of which he and his countrymen had already supped full. The next day, whitsun Eve, when Egmont's head fell upon the Market- place of Brussels, the portrait-painter to the Duke of Alva died, an unintended victim to the Same sentence of death. Heart and brain might well succumb to a shock which startled all Europe. The wail which rose from the crowd in the Grande Place, echoed from the folks within doors all through the city, it brought tears of excitement td the eyes of Alva and his soldiery, it roused a country to rebellion. With the great tragedy the lesser one is associated. Who knows what fear, beset the painter for himself, for his dearest friends?• When he heard the words of the condemnation they were a revelation to him. If the great ones of the earth were not safe before injustice, he might ask how much of justice had there been in the burnings and slayings of the past six months, in which many good Catholics had trustingly half acquiesced? If tlie Protestant Hoorn should rightly suffer for his heresy, yet what reason could suffice to condemn the loyal Catholic Egmont, Who had himself helped to burn and slay with fanatic fervour in the cause of the Catho- lic Church? It was enough to make the most devout cherish doubts of the piety of the Government. Of what qualms of Protestant questioning may have as- sailed mind in that last twenty-four hours of his lire, we have no record, only the story goes that he con- fided the terrible secret to a trusty friend, and died upon the same day as Egmont and Hoorn. To-day the memory of the patriot nobles is honoured in bronze upon the square of the Sa,blon' and their fellow-victim's por- trait of their murderer hangs upon the walls; of the public picture gallery a few hundred yards away.—" The Magazine of Art, February. The leader of the Opposition offered a Council. ' few remarks, the Address was agreed to, and the business of the Session went forward. What takes place now the reader of the news- paper can see for himself, though I am not quite sure that the enormity of the infliction is fully ap- prehended. Thp House has now been sitting a week. But as a matter of fact the real debate on the Address has not yet commenced. In the House of Commons debates always turn upon in amend- ment, and of the imposing list of amendments of which notice has been given the first his ifot yet been reached. What has taken place during all these dreary days since the Address; was moved has been a kind of preliminary canter. We shall go over all the ground again as the various amend- ments come up. For all practical purposes the House might have' been closed up to to-day, or on the other hand the debate might close to-day, .the subject matter of most of the amendments having °been fully discussed. The sturdy iteration of the -speeches, and the knowledge that we shall have them all over again before the Address is voted, has lead a depressing 'effect upon the House. ,But the proceedings have been illumined by one or two speeches. Mr. Glad- stone contribution to the debate was notable in more ways than one, It might be thought that the House of Commons was, by this time, fully ac- quainted with his capabilities and-not prone to be astonished by any fresh development. As a matter of fact his speech of last Thursday is yet talked of, especially among new Members struck with tlie grace of manner of its delivery, the felicity of its phrasing, the force of its argument, and the transcen- dent personal superiority established over any other individual in the House. There is a generous desire to make the most of Mr. W. H. Smith' but it is Piti- ful to think of him as i leader of the House, stand- ing up against Mr. Gladstone. Lord Randolph Churchill's speeches form the other event of the week The second was by far the better, the noble lord being delivered from the quite unaccustomed load of nervousness which rather weighted him on Thursday night. Not a day has passed without supplying its evid- enc's in support of the warning with which the "Daily News" on Monday week electrified the world. The calling out of the German Reserves was promptly followed by the publication in the semi-official "Berlin Post" of an article which, in its effect upon the foreign Bourses, eclipsed the earlier note of alarm. There is a very natural and commendable desire on the part Of the English Press to speak as softly tie possible of the signs Of war, which make Europe at the present moment 'reverberate with the sounds of preparations. But the policy of the ostrich in presence of danger has always ben ridiculed. It is no use burying our heads in the sand, and saying there will be no war, because we deprecate the misery and horror that war entails. We must face facts, and though we may still go on.hoping for the best,facts gather in a gloomy cloud. War may ultimately be avoided' But this is beyond dispute, that things cannot for many weeks longer go on as they are proceeding. There must be very shortly either an understanding or a misunderstanding between France and Germany. War, itself, would be hardly more costly, or lead to more anxiety than does the present condition of active preparation. The Queensbury divorce case went off With a quietness that by contrast with an earlier case was partieluarly delightful. It is a pity that the Mar- quis will not let well alone, but insists upon writ- ing to the papers. lie is a curious man, scion of a odd family, of which Lady Florence Dixie is One of the most unexceptionable specimens. The last that was heard of the Marquis of Queensbury before he came into the Divorce Court was from San Fran- cisco, where he was engaged in religious contro- versy on the platform with Monsignor Capel. div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
HER DARL/NG HAND.

It was the end ,of July, and the furlough of Captain Herbert Morgan' of the Bombay and Baroda Regiment, would expire in October. What was he to do with the rest of it.? London law so scorched and befouled by sun and dust as to be no longer possible—so abanoned by all as to oblige even the gentle Hindoo of gt. James's Square to leave his broom by the lamp-post and drift down to the sea.

But where was the Captain to go? There is, perhaps, but little to choose between Brighton and Scarborough. Margate and Eastbourne' To him they were all dreary places alike: all full of dreary people drearily amusing themselves. Not in England, then, would he stay. Rather would he cross the Channel. There, at all events, the festive nigger with) his jingling banjo, the blatant tub-thumper with his blasphemous jeremaids, and the British Philistine with his smug respectability and con- genial belongings, are not at home. Boulogne, Dieppe, Trouville—which of them should it be? The first and last he had already done. Dieppe only:was new to him: he would try that. Accordingly he alighted next aay at the Hotel de Londres just _4l time for dinner. When he entered i the mak the table d'hote was in full swing. There was but one vacant chair; this he promptly occupied. Some men on these occasions study the menu first and the room afterwards. Herbert Morgan reversed the operation. With a swift survey of the latter, he obtained a decided impression that there was only one good-look- ing woman in the room, and that she was sitting next to him—on his right. This made him happy. Then he read the menu and saw that it was good, which made -him happier still. Meanwhile he had become conscious that he was under the examination of a big gentleman of about forty, years of age, whose bullet head was orna- mented with a thick crop of short, briskly black hair, a pair of elephantine ears, a brace of eyes beadlike and restliass, and an enormous ebony moustache beautifully waxed at the ends. The appearance of this personage, who was sitting on the other side of his fair neighbour, and evidently her friend, was decidedly fierce, and sug- gested to the mind of the Captain an idea. "I wonder," thought he, "if I am so highly favoured by fortune as to have come across a specimen of those terrible beings I have so often heard of, who are never known to spare a Than in their anger or a woman in their love? C,ertainly,`he looks for all the world just like one. It might be worth while to draw him; he ought to show sport." As soon as dinner was over, an elderly lady on the other side of the gentleman made a move to the door, followed by him and his neighbour. The regular features the wavy brown-gold hair, and the musical voice of the latter had, at the very first, aroused in a nature ever susceptible to the influence of beauty unbounded ad- miration' which reached enthusiasm when the cunning curves of her full though supple figure revealed them- selves to him in her progress round the room. For the first time in his life he had a presentiment that he was under the influence of one of those women to whom the power is given, or attributed by their slaves, to mortify or revivfy the hearts of men, and he yielded without a struggle to the feeling. "0, what a divine creature 1" he exclaimed half aloud. "Who in the world can she be? No matter; whatever may be the cost I'll win her, the whole world, and the bullet-headed man included, notwithstanding." Strong emotions are apt to impress themselves on the human countenance. In his case they did so deeply, for the bullet-headed man glared at him ;furiously as he passed out "Confound the fellow !" muttered the Captain, "he need not be in such a mortal hurry to be jealous; I have not even begun operations." Herbert soon learnt that the ladies were Madame and Mdlle. de Lisle of Guadaloupe, and that the gentleman with them was a nephew of the former—Achille Leroy, Colonel M Chasseurs d'Afrique—on leave. He, the Captain, had too much tact to address his neighbour without sufficient justification, and was far too thin- skinned to risk a snub. So he waited. But, alas; things looked even more unpromising on the following day. For the gallant Colonel, evidently suspicious of danger, had changed places with his cousin. But opportunities rarely fail to come to those. who know how to wait and when to dare. -

Probably the bathing at Dieppe is as promiscuous a performance as anywhere. along the coast of France; at all events, it is a pretty sight enough there. So on the beach every forenoon, above. .the merry multitude floundering, in the sea, all the visitors assembled, includ- ing Madame de Lisle and the Colonel. There they sat by the hour, throwing stones into the sea, when they were not watching the fair Marie conquering the crests of the amorous waves until she found herself far away from the shore. Too far sometimes for safety. On these occa- sions the gallant Colonel fidgeted himself into a fever. For minutes together he would stand pale with fear and anger, with his glasses glued to his eyes, looking out to sea. Then he would dash them ? down passionately, violently declaiming the while against the foolhardiness, &c., of women in general, and of Mario in particular. His apprehensions, as it proved, were .not ill-founded. For one fine morning, as he was watching her, she did suddenly disappear. A cry of horror then broke from his lips, and he rushed to the shore. But of what use to a drowning woman is a colonel who can't swim. He cried for help; but in vain. There seemed no means of deliverance from the maw of the cruel sea. Yet, stay; whose is that brown head close by the spot where she has sunk? It disappears as he watches it. When it returns to the surface there is something more than a man's head visible. There is a woman's form. He has saved her. "Bless him!" shout again and again the 'mob in chorus, mad with excitement. Soon they near the shore. Then the man touches ground, carries his

div.p: A CENTENARIAN GANDER: FOUNDED
ON FACT. (Frortt "The Blackburn Times.")

Perhaps no biped, with the exception of man himself, has been more belauded than the goose, and though they both (one in life and the other in death) oe,sssionally re- ceive a good basting, it is no doubt because they richly deserve it; it does them both good, and the opera- tion often has a mollifying effect upon the stomach of one, and the temper of the other; but in the rase of the goose which fOrms the subject of this sketch, his hide was so impenetrable, or as %scientists call it-pachyder- matous, that even at the very latest stages of the abor- tive cooking operation "goose-grease" would not per- colate through his tanner-like skin; and this caused an inquiry to be instituted into his chequered career which revealed the fact that he was a reputed centenarian. Geese will, it is known, attain, in common with eagles, elephants, and ravens, to a patriarchal age, if they are pets, or escape the vicissitudes of early training, and many fruitless attempts have been made to ascertain upon their decease,. as in unfeathered bipeds, the date of birth of birds of this genus which were almost beyond the dissector's cleverest .manipulation, even if provided with the best Sheffield cutlery. Copster.Green (which also rejoices in another vulgar title—Goosemuck Hillock) was assigned by tradition as the earliest haunt of this bird which spreads desolation and barrenness all around its lairs in life, but somehow has been written and sung and spoken of in death even greater than its merits; but this bird being of a breed capable of great fattening powers had been re- moved from time to time to many other great breeding grounds in Ribble valley, with a view to perpetuate the species. So it came to pass that when the stud-book of the oldest inhabitant's Memory came to be ransacked he had also been seen gambolling at Hurst Green for a

div.p: iolettgthe- \-1' for bqu,

~..pened period; he had frolicked abautLaneho Green a course of seasons; Samlesbury Green had wit- nessed his antics for many Michaelmases ; Knowle Green could bear testimony to the frights he had occasionally given to the riotous schoolboys in that famous locality; in' act,there was not a common in the dietrictbut could of having pastured some of his innumerable de- 'As at some time or other; or a resident who had pt ft. his melodious (?) cackle. But near last Christmas he was missed suddenly from the neighbourhood of Dutton; the rural policeman, the village cur, the country postman, Mr. Fenton's tame- keepers, the local preacher, the mischievous schdolboy ; those who had said "he never would be missed," they all missed him. And the news spread as far as Black- burn on the market-day; and the "active and intelli- gent" members of the local police force/were asked to keep a special look out for his well-known form, dead or alive,; they did not require his photograph or a written description, such as appears in the "Hue and Cry" for a noted character, his size and weight, not to speak of his bullet-proof cuticle being sufficient evidence to warrant hie immediate detection. It would be difficult, if not dangerous, to detail the manner of his death, and how his remains were ab- ducted or transhipped to Blackburn just at that season of the year when "goose clubs" are being wound up; suffice it to say that this identical bird lay in a secure spot behind the "Bird-i'th'-Hand," in Bolton-street. waiting for a sufficient number of shillings being de- posited before he could be disposed of in a raffia. Men ' with "silly shillings" wire scarce that season' and mine host, who was engmeerihg the affair, was at his wits'- end how to get up a sufficient number of subscribers before the carcase got "too high" in flavour. Some desperate expedients were resorted to, notably "penny shakes ;" that is, twelve persons laid each a penny down, and "ricked off," which won a share; but this did not realize shares fast enough. As a last resource "Rob," as we will christen 'him; adopted a rather risky expedient for brin'ging the matter to an end by putting some names down of men whom he thought could be depended upon to pay him after he explained that he knew that they had once won something when other people had put their names on the paper. One of these dependable men happened to be a certain brick and tile maker, who lived in the country, and occasionally called at the "Bird" on a market-day, but who for a few weeks had omitted to look in. At last the raffle came off, with all the excitement which the size of the fowl, the heavy shaking, and the October brew could add to the occasion. Some of the shakers who had "never won owt P ther life" emptied the dice into the bowl as if they were dispensing, medicine, they did it so care- fully; another would dexteiously.remove the box from the right hand to the left, and 'dash them on the bottom of the dish with, , the nonchalance of a professional conjuror. Thirty had been got in three shakes by "Rob" himself, and he wore a look like a wreath of • roses, and felt a good deal relieved about some of the shillings he was sponsor for. When it hadvt down to the last shake or two an old gentleman with a crooked finger on his right hand, reputed to be very lucky' though his hat looked as if he baii-penspired.fredy in it many summers, volunteered to I shale for the brielimaker, whose name was down inn- I known to him. He rattled thirty-foux off 'the Alice in quicksticks, a thing he had never done for himself, and I shortly after that number was declared to be the winner of the 20-pound goose or gander. , Bob, who had been speculating on a " clean book" now set his wits to work how to approach Yorky, the brickmaker, whose temper is a little hasty, and who has a nasty habit of speaking his mind. He thought once of cooking the goose for his customers, inviting Yorky, and getting forgiven for his practical joke whilst every-, body was in good humour. But he concluded to run no risk, but see him next morning before some of his cronies advised him of his luck. Early next day, for the state of the bird was getting critical, Rob might have been seen loitering past the tile works as if he had been taking a constitutional in that direction, and had no sinister object in view. He fortunately found Yorky on the ground, and after passing a few compliments he carelessly introduced the subject of the raffle, and told him not that it had come off, but that he had taken the liberty of putting him down for a shilling share, ex- pecting that Yorky would refuse to pay, on the ground that he had not been consulted, but contrary- to his usual fiery custom he paid the money without a murmur, and then Rob had to acquaint him with the fact that it had been won for him, a thing which Yorky said he ought to I have told him at once, without shirking the subject in I any way, witli'divers other remarks unsuitable for ears I polite. The same day the goose arrived at Yorky's, and his patient wife undertook to cook it if possible. From its size and the thickness of its epidermis she concluded it would be a toughish task, and resolved in her own mind to do her utmost to make it tender and palatable. To that end she decided to boil it first and then roast as usual, trusting to sharp teeth and sharper knives for a satisfactory demolition of this Methuselah in feathers. Meanwhile, as it had come to hand so easily and cheaply, Yorky, who was not in the secret about its extraordinary longevity, proceeded to invite a few friends to the feast, among whom were the village schoolmaster and his wife, who along with all the neigh- bours had heard about the arrival of the bonny bird. ; The/ eventful night having arrived, and all being I seated round the mahogany, Yorky planted himself at 1 the head, and flourished his knife and fork like an old practitioner, feeling at the knife-edge as if he had not spent half-an-hour on the back-door step sharpening it till bethought it would "cut through the bone an' all." Plunging the fork through the centre of its broad back, as if he had been spearing a salmon, he tried to feel his way through the upper crust without ‘pauch apparent exertion, but by the-tirne he had reached the tendons and endeavoured to dissever a leg, beads of perspiration rose on his manly brow, and the mixture of " chaff " and commiseration to which he was treated by his guests did not help him much when he tried the other leg; so be twisted his dish a little and essayed ,to take a nice slice or two from the breast, when, sad to relate, the application of pressure all-at one end caused the fowl to fly, or rather flutter, right off the greasy dish on to the parlour floor. Instead of lifting it upon the dish, and apologing for his clumsiness, he at once gave the com- pany a literal intdrpretation of the famihar expression called "Shoeing" a goose; not as it is depicted in such rude fashion upon one of the gargoyles of Whalley Church; but applied "leather to leather," as he put it' after he had recovered his temper; just as Jimmy 'Brown used to do when kicking from the corner flag for goal. No, he could not resist inflicting one terrific kick of vengeance upon the defunct gander, and as it struck the casing of the parlour door, and dropped with a thump upon the hollow floor, he found that he had in- deed " kocked the stuffing out of him." His careful and patient wife however picked the carcase up, and as she scraped up the sage and onions, which were splashed across the door like a trowelful of mortar, and placed them 'carefully back in the original receptacle, she assured him that what was sauce for the goose was ditto for the gander, and he might kick it as he liked "he'd have it to eat." He retorted that, although ,he was a Yorkshire-bite, it would be "too tough a job for him to tackle," &e., &c. After the commotion created by Yorky's exhibition of temper, upon his discovery of the extreme age of the goose, had subsided, a makeshift meal was provided, and the conversation naturally kept in the same groove. The schoolmaster had heard of the sudden dis- appearance of this antiquated fowl, which tradition said "Old Balshaw " used to' clod stones at" when a boy, for hissing so spitefully at him, when waddling at the head of his harem across Copster Green, and, as he said, if this was the same bird, there was no wonder at its becoming fossilised, for Balshaw had been dead since Feb. 4, 1881, and he was certainly above one hundred years old. Others in the company also commented upon the coincidence, and the general concensus of opinion was that, be it goose or be it gander, it was practically indigestible if allowed to live above a cen- tury, and that its reduction to "dust" would be a big task for Dame Nature herself. However, the record of its stay on earth ends here. • W. HIIIXE.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM. Mr. Chamber- lain addressed a meeting of his constitgents in the Birming- barn Town Hall on Saturday night. After referrin4to the change in the position of the Irish question since 1885, he said they were told that nothing could be done for the people of England, of Scot!And, or of Wales, until they had completely satisfied the demands of 85 Irish members of the so-called National party. That was a hard saying, and he was not prepared to accept it. He did not admit that the terms of the settlement were to be dictated by a portion of tbe Iriab representatives. The measures for which Liberals fought In 1885 were even more urgent now, and they must not and should not be indefinitely postponed because the Irish lead- ers were demanding an impracticable form of government which would be as injurious to them as it would be danger- ous to Great Britain. It would no doubt be a glorious achievement for any statesman Or any party to Rive peace to Ireland and eternity to the United Kingdom, bat it would be still more glorious to our patriot- ism, to our capacity for government, and to our free institu- tions, if, by putting aside party passion and party prejudice all sections could combine to seek and find a solution of this great historic problem, and relieve us from the per- petual nightmare of Irish disaffection. div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
ROUSE OF LORDS Mormer.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15. The Cathedral Churches Bill was introduced by the Bishop of Carlisle, and read a first time.

A PHER'S RIGHTS. Replying to Lord Ribblesdale, Lord COLERIDGE re- peated the opinion he gave in the recent action against Lord Graves, that it was competent to try a peer by a common jury where that peer waived his right to be tried by his peers. The LOUD Citaxmcr.r.on gave a contrary opinion—that a peer was not competent to waive his right to be tried by his peers—though he did not wish to be dogmatic. Lord HERSCHELL considered that Lord Coleridge had, as was customary with the judges, decided on the spur of the moment, but he remarked that the weight of authority seemed to be against the noble and learned Lord.

The Women's Suffrage Bill of Lord Denman was re- jected without a division, Lord SALISBURY having pre- viously pointed out that it was not usual for either House to undertake legislation for the purpose of alter- ing the constitution of the other House. ' Their lordships adjourned at 5 35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mowner.

The speaker took the chair at 4 0. A new writ was moved for St. George's, Hanover- square, by Mr. Akers-Douglas, the chief Conservative whip. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, as an elector, objected in order to give more time to the constituency. The House divided : For the issue of the writ, 173; against, 93; majority, 80. The writ was therefore issued.

THE LONDON COAL AND WINE DUES.-Mr W. H. SMITH informed Mr. Buxton that the Government ad- hered to the decision of Lord R. Churchill in regard to the renewal of the coal and wine dues, but reminded him that the late Chancellor of the Exchequer bad invited the inhabitants of the district affected to make their wishes known to Parliamentl through their repre- sentatives. .

FaiPLOTERS' LIAIIILITY.—Mr. W. H. SMITH stated that it was the intention of the Government to propose egis- ionlat this session dealing with the question of employers' bililiaty for injury to their workpeople.
THE ADDRESS.

The debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. BEAD- LAMA, who, referring to the passage in the Queen's. Speech stating that there was no apprehension of any disturbance of European peace, asked how that state- ment could be reconciled with the apprehensions ex- pressed by the Premier and the ex-Chancellor of the Exchequer. He asserted that the country was against war, and was opposed to any interference in affairs with which We had no concern. The hon. member criticised the policy of the Government in the affairs of Egypt and Ilurmith, and asked why Lord R. Churchill when in office refused to listen .to the proposals of the Burmese Ernheasy in Paris. Dealing with the affairs of Ireland, he asked if it could be wondered that the people wha suffer from the system of evictions hated us, and inquired if the Government had any real inten- tion of bringing in a bill for the reform of 'local govern- ment in Ireland upon a popular basis. He described with a few vigorous touches an eviction at which he had been preSent, as one of a troop of Dragoons, to accom- plish the removal of a dying man and a mother and two children, the subsequent death of the man, and of how a few night§ afterwards, standing on sentry, he was aroused by a moan close by, and how he found the woman dead, with a dead child hanging to her breast. Lord R. Ontatenrix said it would be improper on his part to go at any length into lote foreign policy of the Government, but he Would say that he read with the utmost satisfaction and.entireapproval the instructions which the Government had sent to Sir William White; and if the negotiations were conducted in the spirit of those instructions, the effect would be to entirely set aside all difficulties, and bring about a settlement of affairs in tile Balkan Peninsula. As to why he neglected, R Secretary for India, to negotiate with the Burmese Embassy when it visited Paris, it was impossible for him to db so, as the Embassy had come to negotiate with the French Government for a fresh protectorate or alliance with the King of Burman, ostensibly directed against,the British Government. Referring to the Glenbeigh evic- tions, the noble lord said he defied lion. members to find a case more favourable to the landlords. With very few exceptions they had acted a generous, humane, and patriotic part. He saw nothing specially alarming in the state of Ireland, at the present tim,e. After warmly defending the Chief Secretary's administration of Ire- land, Lord Randolph proceeded to refer to the plan of compaig,n, remarking that he never was much altrmed t•by it. The great struggle for the Union he regarded, so far as Ireland was concerned, as absolutely over, but it was not over in England; there it had still to be fought out. His Lordship 'ex- amined the various ways of miiintaining the Union from tils own 'point of view, and said the conclusion he had arrived at was that the right way to maintain the Union was to identify the Government of the Union and the party of the Union in the minds of the English people with good, creditable administration, and wise and progressive legislation; and if, 'unfortunately they became identified . with the , reverse of this, down would go' the Government, the party, and the Union, to which they professed to be so devoted. He con- fessed that he regarded the Liberal Unionists as, kind of Useful crotch, and it was to the Tory party he looked for the maintenance of the Union. Alluding to Mr. Chamberlain's action, he said he tknugbt he was pursuing an erroneous course, and that no member on the Government side of the House would follow him in a line of policy which would in any way lead to the constitution in Dublin of anything in the nature of an Irish Parliament. Noticing the passage in the Royal Speech which .stated that the Estimates had been framed with a due rezard to economy and eroctency, uoru ilanct.vit• sant ft they nan they must have greatly altered since be left the Cabinet. He suggekted tllat Ministers when bringing in ..the Estitnates,. should, instead of reading a lengthy speech prepared by the Department,' cireulate with the Esti- mates some days before their discussion a written state- ment enabling Members to deal with the facts of the case. He •would •alsb suggest that the Estimates after the first vote be 'sent to a committee to ba thoroughly sifted. Alluding to the question of coaling stations, he said he never resigned on that question, but on retrench- ment. Ile was very far from being an advocate of cowardice. but be insisted ' upon such a foreign policy as would obviate the necessity of increased expenditure, and challenged, the Govern- ment, if they intended to add to their naval and military resources, to'dO .so by revising the system of taxation, and4etting the ,people feel the practical resulteof such a policy. As to the criticisms of his friends, it Was not the first time he had had to wrestle with 'the' Tory party Four years ago he so displeased the party that hardly a Conservative member in the House would so much as give him a nod of recognition. Again there appeared all the chargei of disloyalty and treachery, hut be appealed to the tribunal oft hoe and to the just and•generous Judg, meat of the people. = • Sir J. M'KENNA made some remarks in defence of his action as a landlord; and Mr. J. F. O'BRIEN and Mr. ABRAHAM continued the debate rind vindicated the plan of campaign from the Nationalist point of view. Mr. LIMA: Maintained that the Glenbeigh evictions were not exceptional. They degraded the law and pre- vented the maintenance of order, and he protested against the forces of the Crown being employed to carry them out. _

Lord E. HAMILTON, throwing all the blame for the evictions on the National League, aroued.that during the present winter the landlords had 'done all in their power to avoid evictions. •He dwelt upon the impossi- bility of distinguishing between tenants who could not pay and those who could,.and enlarged upon the desk- ability of compulsorily making the •tenants become owners of their holdings. -

_ Mr. SHAW.LEFEVRE, V7llO began by a 'vigorous fustifica.. tion of Lord It. Churchill's resignation, dimmed at some length the Army and Navy Estimates, and supported the proposal to leave to a Committee the consideration oi items of naval and military expenditure. Adverting to theXgyptian campaign, he failed to see that anyadvan- tag& had been gained by the occupation.of that.copiatry to anyone but the bondholders; and with regard- to Ire- land, he pointed out that the action of the Chief Secretary in advising the landlords to reduce their .rents clearly proved that his views had changed. He denied that the agrarian question, was the only difficulty. Ho gave a qualified approval to the plain of campaign, and, expres. sing no surprise at the tenants combining under the cir- cumstances, contended that their action was quite as justifiable as the recent agitation of the Welsh farmers to avoid the payment of tithes. Mr. CirszoN said the word coercion was a 'nickname adopted by the Opposition for any measure intended to repress crime, but he believed that the measures that the Government /were to bring forward for the amendment of legal procedure was to be of general and permanent application. He regretted that Lord Randolph Churchill had described the LiharaLTEninniat. ',arty a aernteh,-lanolitArl—an4

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 5, 1887
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 5, 1887

maintained that it was not true or cornplimentary("Oh, oh," and laughter)—the Unionist party was a staff— (laughter)—to the Conservative party, and he hoped they would walk with the Conservative party per- manently. (Laughter) He condemned the plan of cam- paign, which was designedly an attack upon landlords and upon the Government Of this country. Mr. Issnotrannas vindicated the plan of campaign, and discussed, in a sarcastic vein, the position of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain, and the probable re- sults of the Round Table Conference. Lord \VOMITER congratulated Mr. Labauchere on being the only English Radical who had dared openly to sup- port the plan of campaign, and in the course of a severe criticism of Lord It. Churchill's "insult to Liberal Unionists" drew attention to the discrepancies in his speech that evening as compared with what he said at Dartford. The debate was then adjourned on the motion of Lord G. Hamilton. • • The Supreme Court of Judicature (Irejand) Bill was read a second time, and The House adjourned at 1-15. HOUSE OF LOlWS.7—Tinisisay. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. IRISIT SOLICITORS.—Lord Frrzonnesri laid on the table a bill to amend the law relating to solicitors in Ireland, and it was read a first time. SUGGESTED STATE-AIDED EMIGRATION FOR LONDON UNEMPLOYED.—Lord DENMAN presented a petition in favour of State-aided emigration, signed by eleven gentlemen, who referred to the fact that many men were wandering about the metropolis without work, while there was plenty of wisak for them in the colonies. Their lordships rose at 4 30 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TvEsuay. The Speaker took the chair at .4 0 p.m. , licrrress.—Mr. Curhon, to call attention bathe desir- ability of the attendance of certain members in either House otParliament. • Mr Sexton, that day four weeks, , to call attention to the system of jury-packing pursued by her Majesty's Government in Ireland. (Irish cheers.) Mr: Beton, that day four weeks, to move for a Select Committee on Church revenues. EVACUATION OF PORT HAMILTON. Answering to Mr. Bryce and other members, Sir J. FERGUSON said Port Hamilton will shortly be evacuated by her Majesty's forces. No arrangements have been made respecting its future custody, but it is understood that a Corean official will be present at the time of the departure of the British ships. ,No conditions have been made with the Corean Government, but her Majesty's Government did not determine to retire from Port Hamilton till they pad received a guarantee from the Government of China that no port of Core,a including Port Hamilton, will be occupied by any foreign Power. Her Majesty's Government acted under naval advice when they decided to leave Port Hamilton. Papers on the subject will shortly be presented to Parliament. TRADE wrrn 'THE Sonnass—ln reply to Mr. Bryce, Sir Jas. FERGUSON said lie was not aware that any resolu- tion was taken by her Majesty's Government last July to allow trade with the Soudan to be reopened, but they had been very desirous that this should be done so soon as it should appear that its effect would be beneficial. Since last July the approach of a hostile force to the Egyptian outposts on the Nile rendered a postponement necessary, but since October trade has been generally reviving in the neighbourhood of "Suakim, and the Government had now assented to the proposal of the Government of Egypt to allow trade to be reopened in the Nile valley—of course excluding traffic in arms and ammunition—and orders to that effect will no doubt be I immediately issued by the Egyptian authorities. THE JURIES IN IRISH GOVERNMENT PROSECUTIONS.— In answer to Mr. Stansfeld, the ArroaxEr-Grantnat explained that the Crown Solicitor in Ireland, in direct- ing jurors to stand by, acted upon general directions applicable to all criminal prosecutions. These direc- tions had been in use for many years, and formed part of the instructions given to the solicitor when taking office. According to these directions, of which he had no objection to lay a copy on the table of the House, the solicitor for the exercise of the right of challenge by ' the Crown procured a`full list of the jury panel from the sheriff sometime before a trial, and made due enquiry as to whether any, person thereon • would be likely, from affinity to - the accused or from any bodily or mental infirmity, or from• other cause, to be hin- dered from giving an impartial verdict; and with due caution, acting with promptitude and decision, he was directed to order such jurors to stand by.—ln answer to Mr. T. P. O'Connor, the ATTORNET:GENERAL denied that the directions were ever interpreted to mean that Catholics should not try a Catholic prisoner.—ln answer to Mr. Sexton, he said these did not rest on sta- tutory authority. Mocztnaissons QUESTIONS.—In reply to Mr. Egerton Hubbard, Mr. RITCHIE said the question of the relief of personal its well as real property was occupying the serious attention of Government, but the Government could not commit themselveS to the adoption of any recommendations of the Commission of Agriculture of 1881-2. As it svasa matter that had relation to the pro- posals for local gevernment he could not now give any more information.—ln answer to Mr. Henniker Heaton, Mr. RATERS explained that a postal connection with France for connecting the , parcels post of the two coun- tries was signed in June, and awaited the approval of the French Charnber.—ln answer to Mr. H. J. Wilson, Mr. STANHOPE said that the War Office had no informa- tion as to the truth or otherwise of a statement recently made in a London journal that "the Contagious Diseases Acts are in full force in the most shameful way in Egypt wherever our troops are stationed ;" but he would ask the generalofficer in command to report on the subject.

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The debate on the address was'resumed by Lord G. HAMILTON, who rose amid Ministerial Cheers Referring to the question of expenditure, the noble lord said his noble friend, Lord IL Churchill, had proposed' that the returns of the Admiralty and War. Office, with the estimates of expenditure, should be circulated amongst members, instead of being introduced to the House in the form of a speech. To this the Government had no objection if such were the desire of the House, but otherwise it was not their desire to disturb the existing arrangement. The second proposal of the noble lord was that the Army and Navy eatimates should be referred to a committee. Ailo 'this it might be Worth consideration whether such a step should be taken, blit he certainly thought it would be unwise to refer the accounts of the two departments to a select 'committee of that House, inasmuch as it would be irnpoallible tor such a body to go thoroughly through those accounts in any reasonable number of years. His own department was one which expended a large sum of money, and he hardly knew what would be the effect of a sudden and large reduction of estimates in that department. Looking at the number of men employed on continuous service, and the contracts that had been entered into by the Government the result of any kuch step would be to leave a larger number of men in a-condition of idleness. He believed that if it were possible to get over the initial difficulties, and to appoint such a committee as had been asked for, that committee would be astonished at randaratirm a the demo.nria mad/.be tba Admiralty. In considering this question the House must bear in mind the enormous indrease that had taken place in the mercantile marine of Great Britain; which had doubled its tonnage within the last ten years, and must not forget that with a commerce showing nothing like a proportionate advance, the mai", expenditure of the great Powers had during that period increased 50 per cent., as against an increase of only 16 per cent. in the case of Great Britain. It was absolutely necessary that Great Britain should keep pace with what was going on among neighbonring countries. (Hear, hear.) To appoint the committee asked for would in reality be to tie the hands of the Government if it were understood that they were to adeept any conclusions the committee might arrive at—a thing which no Government could do consistently with its responsibilities. Turning to the Irish question, the noble lord announced the inten- tion of the Government to do nothing to alienate the assistance of those allies who had enabled them to secure the unity of the kingdom. (Cheers and counter cheers.) He concluded by a high eulogium on the self-sacrifice and patriotism of hon. members opposite who had acted with the Government in assuring so great an end. Mr. Childers followed on the financial question, and, eli- citing from Lord R. Churchill the information that the committee he desired was not to be an annual committee, hut one that would once for all examine and thoreughly overhaul the estimates, gave the noble lord the member for Paddington his hearty support.—Mr. Chaplin brought the debate back to the Point of personal interest by undertaking to chastise Lord Randolph for the injury he had done to the cause of the Union. He did not spare his references to "the wilful, ietractable, and almost impossible disposition" of the noble lord, or to the explanations of afamons resig- nation "every other day," or to what he would call the " clap•trap " of certain speeches it it were not that he did not wish to use that name.—Mr. Conybeare next bad his opportunity of expressing his feelings on the Glenbeigh , evictions.—Mr. Schwann rather staggered the House with the 'ingestion of a wooden-legged support, and Mr. C. Graham attached to the Liberal dissentients the unkind ap- pellation of crutch-and-toothoiek gentleman.—After Mr. Duff had given the debate an Admiralty flavour, the mem- ber for Stockport (Mr. Jennings) warmly took up Lord Ran. dolph's cause, vouched for his popularity, and resented "the outburst of splenetic malevolence" heard earlier in the evening. Sir W. Lawson, in We characteristic vein, hailed Lord Randolph as a reformed character who had forsworn wild ways and taken the pledge of peace. Mr. T. W. Rus- sell defended the owners of Glenbeigh, and Mr. Wallace es- poused the Plan of Campaign. Subsequently, Mr. Smith had his first argument with Parnellites as to the adjourn- ment of the debate. The latter prevailed, and the debate stood adjourned on the motion of Mr. H. Cosshani. The Hones adjourned at twenty minutes to one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve. THE ADDRESS.—Debate on the Address in reply to the Queen's Speech was resumed by Mr. Handel Cossham. who expressed his satisfaction that the first paragraph in the ' Speech was directed to the most important question of peace in Europe. The debate was advanced by a dozen speeches, delivered from all quarters of the House except the front benches, which were comparatively deserted. Radicals re- joiced in the prospect of retrenchment, and announced their continued faith in Mr. Gladstone's plan of conciliation for Ireland. Tories denounced with fervour the Plan of Cam- paign, and, in some instances, expressed a bold opinion

against their late leader's action in leaving the Cabinet ; a Mcotch member waxed eloquent on the means of saving the country's " bawbees;" and Irish members continued their vindication of the Plan of Campaign and denunciation of evictions. Mr. Crilly, as one of the members who take their trial at Dublin next week, particularly distinguished himself by the eloquence of an obvious conviction that he was do. ing.his country patriotic service. . . _

EW BILLS.—Some new Bills, including Mr. Broadhurst's Distress for Rent Bill and Lord Ehrington s Bill for amend, log the registration laws, were brought in, and the House adjourned shortly before six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TRURSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. hfiscumarEors.—Lord Hobhenee brought in a bill to amend the law relating to copyholds, and to facilitate the enfranchisement of copyholders. The bill was read a first time.—The Earl of Mount-Edgcumbe (Lord Steward of the Household) brought up Her Majesty's reply to the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne. It was in these words :—" I thank you for your loyal and dutiful Address. I resort with great satisfaction to your counsel and advice in dealing with the important questions which will be brought before you, and which concern the highest interests of the country and the welfare and happiness of all my sub- jects."—On the motion of Lord Cranbrook the Pluralities Act Amendment Bill was read a first time.

Their Lordships adjourned at half-past four o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THUESDAY. The Speaker took tbe chair at four e'clock. Quirrre RAILWAY, &c.—Sir J. Goan stated that the re- port of a raid upon the Quetta-Pishin Railway by Duranis was wholly without foundation.—The HOME SecnxreatY in- formed the House that he had communicated with the Pre- sident of the Divorce Division, and he hoped he would be I able by rule of Court to check the publication et obj:ction- able reports. • THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. P. Mahoney, who concluded the ad- dress he had commenced on the previous day. Mr. E. Beckett defended the foreign policy of the Government as 11 likely to preserve peace. Having declared that the whole I Tory party was pledged to retrenchment as much as the member for Paddington, he contended that the Government I ought to suppress the National League. Mr. Illingworth considered that the news that the whole Tory party was pledged to retrenchment was the most joyful that had been communicated to the House for some time past. He urged that it was the duty of the Government to do all they could to bring about a better state of feeling on the Conti- nent. He desired that the Irish question should be kept to the fore, and that the battle should go on until a settlement was made.—Mr. A. DUNCOMBE thought both parties might meet together and try to settle the Irish question, for he held that we ought to give Ireland something more than verbal sympathy; and he added that the consideration to which she was entitled had been deepened and intensified by the sorrowful scenes that had lately been witnessed at Gleubeigh. It would, he said, always remain incomprehen- sible to him that it had been thought consistent with hu- manity to carry out those evictions in the depth of a most rigorous winter —Sir W. C. PLOWDEN, who bad formerly discountenanced the plan of campaign under a mistaken im- pression of its workiog, now witharew his condemnation.— Colonel Notax suggested that the Government might set- tle the Irish difficulty by advancing eine millions to enable the poorer class of tenants, of whom 150,000 held farms of lees than five acres, to double their holdings with land ob- tainable from large grass farms.—Professor STUART defen- ded the plan of catnpaign as resembling in some respects the English trade unions, his contention being that it was because the law in this matter was unjust that the action against it was justifiable. He declared that no Round Table Conference would induce him to abandon the demand for a separate Parliament for that country, with an Execu- tive proceeding from it, unless the Parnellite members should draw back from that to which they had committed themselves.—Mr. CREMER moved the adjournment of the debate. 'rne House adjourned at ten minutes past one o'clock.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. • The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thurs- day forenoon' when there'were present Mr J Lowe (chair- man). Rev TCisambers, Rev Father Finegan, Messrs W Tyrer, W G Ashton, J Fisher, J Buckley, J Whalley, J Leatherbarrow, C B Johnson, P Middlehurst, J Ellison J Ranson, W Swift, E Svder, T Eatock, J Birchall W B Longton, W Daine, T F' Hill, W Gerrard, and S LI Hartley (clerk). STATISTICS LONGEVITY AT THE WOBXIIOI:7SE.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 497 inmates in the Workhouse this week, 495 last week, and 496 in the corres- ponding week last year; 66 vagrants had been relieved, against 36 last year. He also reported that since the last meeting of the Board William Yardley, an inmate stated to be 100 years of age had died.—The Clerk said it was re- po:ted there was a woman at present in the Workhouse who was 102 years of age. She had been in the Workhouse since 1871.

- CRUELTY TO CAILDREN.—The Local Government Board wrote that they were of opinion the Guardians could not contribute three guineas annually to the Liverpool Society for the Preveution of Cruelty to Children. The Clerk Intl- mated that he was still in communication with the solici- tors, and he thought he would ba,able to /how the Local Government Board that it wee competent for them to make the payment.—The Rev T Chambers remarked that the society was an admirable institution. THE ECCLESTON ASSISTANT OVERSEER.—The Clerk read communications from the Local Government Board in re- ference to reports made by the district auditor, in reference to the accounts of Mr. T. Parkinson, the assistant over- seer for the townships of Eccleston and Knowsley. and who was in arrear with the collection of the rates.—The Clerk remarked that at the beginning of January Mr. Parkinson was £4,740 21101 in are ear, but be had since collected £4OB lie 3d, and Mr. Parkinson was hopeful of being able to collect the whole amount during the months of February and March.—The Rev. T. Finegan said the matter had fre- quently been before them, and it was time the Guardians gave a decided expression of their ortinion.—The Clerk read the minutes of the Finance Committee, who met on the 6th &mambo, when Mr. Parkinson's explanations were not considered satisfac,ory.—The • Rev. T. Chambers said Mr. Parkinson had served them well as a relieving officer prior to his , appointment as assistant overseer, and he had done lin work admirably. There was no misapnro priation or embezzlement, bat it was through Mr Parkinson's neglect and apathy., Ile thought the matter might be left over until the next audit,—The Clerk said it was really aa old wound breaking out afresh.—After some further dis- mission, Mr. Elfirton moved that the matter be left in abey- ance until the March audit, and the Rev. Father Finegan seconded the motion, which was carried, with directions to to the clerk to write to Mr. Parkinson, expressing the feel- ing of the Board. PROVISION FOR EIRE.—At a meeting of the special com- mittee of the whole Board on the 31st ult, fel the purpose of discussing the quest* of providing an adequate supply of water in the event of 'fire at the Workhouse, Mr. Gaskin, the St. Helens borough Water engineer, was in attendance, and suggested the procuration of a steam fire engine, mak- ing additional provision for the storage of water, furnishing the hospital With corridor pipes and pumps, and the exten- sion of the present telephonic communication from the relief offide in fit,. Helens to the Town Rail: ,On „9te mo- tionof Mr. W. Middlehuret, seconded by the Rev. T. Cham- bers, if was unanimously resolved " that two tanks be pro- vided; that a steam. fire engine (With water attachment, if considered desirable) and sufficient hose be procured; and/ that Messrs. Lowe, Hill, ,Fisher, Wareing, and Middlehurst, with the Workhouse Mar, be appointed a sub-committee, with full powers to carry out the foregoing."—The thanks of the Board *ere tendered to Mr. Gaskin for his valuable advice and assistance.. _-- .

_ Intunovammers.—The Building Committee, at a meet- ing on the 3rd inst, decided to recommend several streeta- ral improvements with regard to the offices, entrance lodge, Jtc.. and the suggestions were adopted by the Board. COUNTY PRECEPT.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a county precept for £6,064 158 Id, to be paid on or before the 28th inst, in respect of the county rate so far as the Union of Prescot was concerned. The clerk added this was a little lees than the last precept. Pupa hest:warm—The Clerk said be bad received a new fire policy upon the workhouse buildings. The premium was £23 15s 31, and the amount covered was £27,350. THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.—Mr. Nine suggested that the Guardians and friends should subscribe towards ptoviding the inmatee with a good substantial dinner about the month of June in celebration of the Queen's Jubilee.—The sug- gestion was favourably received by the members. This was the principal business.
COMPOUND, for Colds and Coughs. Bold throughout the World. le, j,2s. 9d Kay Bros., Stockport.— ..Mot.
The Bank rate was on Thursday reduced from five to four per cent., after standing at the .former figure for seven weeks.

A result of the Doke of Devonshire's tenantry going be- fore the Land Sub-Commission at Bandon is that about 40 of them got "fair rents" fixed, in nearly every instance reductions of about 30 per cent being made, and yet the Duke is a specially good landlord. Joseph King, a labourer from Norfolk, was finally ex- examined at Marlborough.street Police Court on Thursday on the charge of murdering a woman named Anne Sutton and her infant son. The murders were committed with a razor, and the prisoner offered no plea whatever in defence. It was said that insanity has " been in his family " for generations, but there was no evidence to show that he is otherwise than an exceptionally brutal and malignant mis- creant.

SEVERE GALE.—A westerly gale of unusual severity.has been blowing at Queenstown. A woman was blown off the quay on Thursday morning and drowned. Incoming steamers report that the weather in St. George's Channel last night was terrific. A south-westerly gale of great violence sprang up on the Tyne early on Thursday morn- ing. The moorings of the vessels in Shields Harbour were heavily strained. The steamer Cora Maria, of Cardiff, has arrived in the Tyne after being ashore in Bridling ton Bay. For rough, red, or creamed skin there is nothing equal to " Beetham Glycerine wad Cucumber." A few applications will render the skin delicately soft, smooth, and white, and entirely remove and prevent all roughness, redness, cbaps, Irritation, etc. It pqperves the complexion from the effects of frost, cold winds, and hard water, more effectually than any other preparation.—Bottles, Is,, 2s. ed., of all chemists. Free for 3d extra by sole makers. M. BERTRAM AND Box, chemists, Obeltenham.—Advt.
GENERAL NEWS.

Sir Alexander Campbell has been appointed High Commissioner for Canada in London, in the room of hir Charles Tupper. On Saturday, a child's body was found on the railway bank, near Canterbury, having been strangled by a piece of tape. It is believed to have been thrown from a car- riage window. The High Sheriff of Durham has fixed the execution of Thomson and 11I`Cann, who are lying under sentence of death in Durhare Gaol, to take place at eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, Feb. 16.

Mr. James C. Miche a jeweller, while sitting in Spur- geon's Tabernacle, South London, on Sunday evening, waiting for the service to begin, was noticed to fall backwards in his seat, and, on being removed, was found to be dead.

On Saturday afternoon the Prince of Wales, attended by Colonel Teesdale, his equerry-in-waiting and a dis- tinguished party of guests, including Mr. and Mrs. Glad- stone and the Bishop of St. Albans, left St. Pancras for Sandringham. The thief who committed burglaries at Stainton and Carcroft, near Doncaster, last November, it has now been discovered was the notorious Thos. Spencer White, formerly the companion of Charles Peace, the Banner Cross murderer. White is now in York Castle, awaiting trial for a burglary committed in the East Riding.

- - RAID ON COUNTRY INNICEFPNRS.-At Leigh, on Monday, a number of innkeepers were summoned by Superinten- dent Weir under the Food and Drugs Act. The defen- dants were owners of country public houses, and in some cases the spirits supplied to the police were 50 per cent. under proof. Fines from £5 to 10s. were imposed. Several shopkeepers, for adulterating butter, &c., were mulcted in small penalties. A girl, aged 13, named Mary Alice Wharnby, daughter of a collier, of Old-lane, Little Hutton, near Bolton, com- mitted suicide on Saturday night by drowning herself in a pond on a farm near her home. She was a tenter in a cotton mill. Her parents learned that she had been running on a bill for sweets without their consent, and reprimanded her. She did not return home again, but her body was found in the pond on Sunday.

Baron Dimsdale has decided to abandon the Pure Beer Bill of which he gave notice, and to co-operate with Sir E. Birkbeck, who has also a measure before Parliament on the subject. The latter bill is now backed by Sir E. Birkbeck, Baron Dimsdale, Sir S. Crossley, Mr. C. Hall, Mr. Fellowe-s, and Baron Rothschild. Mr. Quilter's bill dealing with the same matter is in no way antagonistic to that of Sir E. Birkbeck, and the two hon. members will give each other mutual support.

TUTS CHAT:BE AGAINST A SISTERTIOOD.—VEHDTCT.— In the Chancery Division, on Monday, Mr. Justice Keke- wich delivered judgment hi the action of Miss Alleard against the Lady Superior of the Protestant Sisterhood of St. Mary at the Cross, to set aside certain deeds under which she gave £B,OOO to the sisterhood. His lordship held that Miss Alleard was fully aware of what she did, and that her gifts were voluntary. He therefore dis- missed the plaintiff's action, with costs. At Manchester, on Monday, Wm. Aseroft, aged 79, was remanded on a charge of counterfeit coining. The other day detectives visited his house, and found the prisoner engaged in coining sixpences. They found mould and battery in full working order, and seized a large number of sixpences which had just been made. They also found a number of shillings which were cooling. The nrisoner admitted his guilt, but said the police ought to have got another man as welL

EXTRAORDINARY PLATE GLASS ACCIDENT.—An extra- ordinary accident occurred on Saturday at New- port, Mon. While a large number of workmen were fixing a large plate of glass, ten feet by nine, in front of some new premises adjoining the Talbot Hotel, the plate fell forward with a crash, which was heard at a distance of several hundred yards. Three men, named Charles Jones, William Hughes, and John Davies were so severely cut that they had to be removed to the infirmary. TEE TITRE Ai:in/aim—A Pontypool correspondent telegraphs that at the Rev. W. Forster's tithe audit for Llanfrechfa, on Saturday, the vicar, after considerable pressure had been brought to bear upon him, consented to grant a reduction of 10 per cent, to those who had been engaged In the agitation for a concession, and to those belonging to the Tithepayers' Association, but only a reduction of 5 per cent, to the non-agitators. This has =sea considerable dissatisfaction amongst the latter class. _ • __

MORS POISONOUS TIMM MPAT.—A death, supposed to be due to eatinw tinned meat, has occurred at Newton Tonney, a in Wiltshire. The father of the deceased (a child aged 17 months) bought a tin of preserved mut- ton, of which his wife, the deceased, and Mr. Shears par- took. All three of these subsequently became ill, and it was found that they were suffering from severe irrita- tion of the stomach. The mother and Mrs. Shears got better, but the child died after bag ill a fortnight, the cause of death being gastritis.

EXTENSIVE WAREHOUSE FIRE fl LONDON.—An ex- tensive fire occurred on Monday inorning at Cohen's rag warehouse, Swan-streot, Southwark, London, at the rear of a large number of shops and dwelling-houses. It was soon evident that the building could not be saved, and the efforts of the firemen were directed to prevent the fire spreading to the surrounding property. The roof fell in, and at two o'clock the place was completely gutted, resulting in the destruction of three buildings of one, two, and four floors respectively, and their con- tents; as well as damage to eight houses in Swan-street and others in Trinity-square and Brockham-stroet ad- joining. The amount of loss is unknown. Messrs. Cohen's premises and contents were insured.

Six BOYS sir AN OPEN BOAT.— On Saturday morn- ing, the steam trawler Malta, of Grantou (Captain Isbister), put into the port with six boys, fpund at sea, in an open boat,,in an exhausted condition. The cap- tain states that ab )ut half-past five this morning, when off May Island, and steaming seawards, he heard cries of someone in distress, and, on looking, saw through the darkness what appeared to be the mast of a boat. He steamed the trawler to windward, and, drifting down on the boat, found it contained six boys, all in a state of mat exhaustion. They were taken on board, and restoratives applied. They stated that they went from Leith in an open boat in the Firth of Forth, and anchored on Ineskeith but the wind drove the boat to seaward. Capt. Isbister says that the boys could not have held out much longer. _ _

Tire Loignox SocrAusrs AT Cul:mm-0n Sunday, the Socialists in London continued their programme of marching to the churches. About 150 members of the Paddington and Bayswater Social Detnocratib Federation attended St. Marylebone Parish Church, where some of the preacher's remarks were greeted with groans and hisses. Eventually, however, all the processionists left the church quietly. 'the contingents of the Kennington, Walworth, and Peckham branches marched to St. Giles's Chbrch, Peckbam, but were refused admission by the police. They then proceeded to Camberwell-green, and their leaders delivered addresses. The Bermondsey Socialists attended the parish church. During the prayers for the Queen and the Royal Family the Social- ists hissed persistently, and greatly disturbed the usual congregation; and it has been stated that proceedings are to be taken against the ringleaders for brawling.

EXTRAORDINARY RECOVERY OY MISSING 14rfolmv.— newspaper vendor, named Cauden, alias Smith, was brought up at Bow-street, on,Mondav, charged with at- tempting to commit suicide. About half-past eleven on , Saturday night the attention of a police-constable was drawn to the prisoner in the lake in St. James's Park. With great 'difficulty the man was rescued in an insen- sible condition. He was removed to the police station. 'where it was found that he was drunk. An emetic 'was administered, 'which had the effect of causing prisoner to vomit four shlllings, a sixpenny-piece, and a half- penny. In reply t 4 Mr. Bridge, the prisoner said that he had sold out his stock of newspapers and had got drunk. He missed his money, and could not understand what had become of it. He therefore threw himself into the water, and now appeared greatly surprised at the sin- gular recovery of his money. He was ordered to find two sureties to be of good behaviour for one month.

MR. MIINDELLA ON THE CONDITION OF TRADE. —Mr. Mundella, M.P., speaking on Monday at a meeting of the Sheffield Chamber of Commerce, said that since .1875 they had experienced a depression in trade, and severe competition, unparalleled in length and universality. That depression and competition had culminated in 1886, the former having been largely owing to over-production. The world, however, didn't go on for any considerable time producing at a loss, and he thought they might reasonably congratu- late themselves that trade had at last touched the bottom. Business was gradually improving, and there would be an increasing margin ot profit The new Spanish Treaty would in the long run be of great advantage in bringing about increased trade. As to fraudulent trading, false marking was a hundred times greater abroad than at home. Lord Stanley of Preston had told hrmhe was bringing in the railway rates bill in the Lords, and would co-operate with him in making it satisfactory. THE CHARGE a LIBELLING A DOCTO73..—At J 3 street, on. Monday, Mr. Heinrich Felbermann, pro- prietor, and Mr. Charles Wilkinson, publisher of Life, were charged with having libelled Dr. Thomas Bird, one of the co-respondents in the recent Campbell Divorce Case, in an article headed "The Cockiolly Bird." Mr. temp, Q.C., in opening the case for the prosecu- tion, described the libel as one of the worst ever pub- lished. The term "Cockiolly Bird," as applied to the complainant by: a certain lady, was a schoolboy expres- sion, meaning simply " a good fellow." The article com- plained of was one giving the supposed instincts of "the Cockiolly Bird," a name applied by Lady Colin Campbell to Dr. Bird. He held that the insinuations were cal- culated to do Dr. Bird grievous professional harm. Nu% Kemp added, that he should not call Dr. Bird un- less the magistrates thought it absolutely necawsary, for it would only gratify his maligners if he were subjected to a repetition of the cross-examination he underwent in the divorce court. Mr. Wonter, for Felbermarua, said that the latter's solicit/1r had written expressing regret that anything should have appeared that had given pain to anyone, and he was there simply to repeat the apology. The defendants were committed for trial. Mr. Wilkinson's recognisanoes in £lOO were taken for his appearance, and Mr. Feltiermann was ordered te etite,r into his own recognisances in Rsoa and find two stiretioi_ in £250 each. A summons was also issued against IN f Durant, the printer of Life, for the same libel.
