div.head: FOREIGN WORKMEN AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: FOREIGN WORKMEN AT ST. HELENS.

THE GLASS TRADE ,DISPUTE. The dispute between the firm of Mersrs. Lyon Brothers, glass bottle manufactures, and their work- men culminated on Saturday afternoon, when in lieu of serving a week's notice the disaffected men were paid a week's wages, and they have not since returned to work. The dispute and its various phases have excited considerable interest through- out the town. The dispute has arisen in reference to the employment of Swedish bottle makers by the firm of Messrs. Lyon. It had its origin some months age in minor differences between the firm and their workpeople. The firm, it is stated, received large orders for bottles made in the same way as bottles manufactured on the continent, and after a lengthy consideration the firm decided to undertake their construction. This proposal .at first met with the approval of the men; but ultimately they came to the conclu- sion that it was neither to the interests of the men nor the manufacturers that the bottles should be made uponthe foreign system, and they declined to proceed with the work. Negotia- tions between the firm and men laving failed, Messrs. Lyon took steps to employ a number of Swedish glassmakers. The bottles, it may be stated, about which the dispute has arisen, are known as "pale wine quarts." The men employed in this kind of work are paid a stated 7sum for producing sixty-two and a half dozen bottles, which complete what is known as a "journey," and upon its com- pletion, which usually takes between five or Aix hours, it has been the habit of the men to go on working, and for this extra work they have been paid so much for every dozen bottles they have pro- duced. Messrs. Lyon Bros. requested their work- men to make these "pale wine quart " bogies after the completion of their ordinary five hours " jour- ney." But this the workmen refused to do. Messrs Lyon Bros. despatched agents to Gothenberg, Christiana, and other places in S weden, and a number of workmen were engaged to proceed to St. Helens. The men allege thnt Messrs. Lyon took no defi- nite action in the matter until December last, when thirty-four men were discharged, in consequence, it was alleged, of the de- pression in trade. It subsequently came to the knowledge of the Glass Bottlemakers' Association that Messrs Lyon were negotiating for Swedish labour. A deputation consisting of Messrs. R Hunter (secretary) and C. Canning was despatched to Sweden for the purpose of laying the facts of the case before the foreign workmen, and, if possible, of preventing their coming to England. The de- putation also went on a similar mission to Ger- many, where, they state, the employers made an , unsuccessful attempt to procure German workmen.l On Saturday last the remaining workmen (about 40 in number) were discharged without notice, as pre- viously stated, but received a week's wages in lieu I thereof. Mr. R. Hunter, the local secretary, has received letters from the Dublin, -Yorkshire, Sun- derland, and Bristol districts, urging the men to I hold out against the masters' demand. Should the dispute continue it is intended to apply to , the trade generally for co-operation and pecuniary I support. ARRIVAL OF THE SWEDES. At half-past three o'clock on Tuesday the Swedish work- men, several of whom were accompanied by their wives, arrived at Lime-street station from Hull. They numbered, about 35, and were immediately escort,d to a Swedish boarding-house in Hardy-street, off Great George-street, where they remained for a few days. It was at first intended to send the men to St. Helens immediately on their arrival, but this was found impossible. A large ware- house nearly opposite the Wesleyan Chapel in Corporation- street, St. Helens, has been prepared for the reception of the Swedes. The building was lately occupied by Messrs. Dodd and Dolton as a silvering works, The large rooms have been partitioned off by Mr. IV. Harrison, builder end coptractor, and made to form about a elczna good-bitea apartments, THE TRADES COUNCIL ON THE

- DISPUTE. A meeting of the St. Helens rades Council was held in the Sefton Arms, Ormskirk-street, on Wednesday night, to consider the action of Mesars.Lyon in introducing foreign workmen into St. Helens. About thirty representatives from various trades were present. Mr. W. Evans, who presided, said if foreigners were allowed to take the place of English workmen in St. Helens the system would extend through that and other districts, as was shown by the intro- duction of foreigners in the north of England, where wages bad in consequence been reduced from 25 to 30 per cent. When the public were acquainted with the plain facts of the case, he was sure they would have full sympathy in en- deavouring to kettle the dispute either by arbitration or otherwise.—Mr. Robert Hunter (secretary to the Bottle Makers' Association) reviewed the history of the dispute. The union did all they could to induce the men to work on, but the men had come to the determination that, no matter what the society did, if the firm introduced foreign labour they would not work in the same factory. (Applause.) There had been a similar occurrence in llnblin, last April, and they were successful in sending the foreigners hack, and with the assistance of the trade, they (the Lancashire members) were going to use every effort to get them off home also. It must be known to all that the introduction of foreign labour in St. Helens not only meant ruination to them as glass bottle makers, but also to other trades —Mr. Jas. Hunter remarked that the dispute would never be set- tled until they got those foreigners to return.—Mr. Canning said statements would be made to the public at a great demonstration en Saturday, which would show clearly how matters stood —Eventually the delegates present decided to assist in the demonstration of Saturday, and if possible get all the other trades to take part. THE FOREIGNERS AT ST:HELENS.

The foreign workmen, with their wives and children, arrived at St. Helens station by the train due from Liver- pool at 3.50 on Thursday afternoon. At that hour some hundreds of persons were congregated in the vicinity of the station, and on the platform' amongst others, were Superin- tendent Johnson, Inspector Keighley, and one or two con- stables, while the foreign workpeople, who travelled from Liverpool in charge of M. Elba Lyon- and an interpreter,. were met by several members of the firm. On leaving the station the crowd gave a lusty cheer and cordially wel- comed the " visitors," some of whop seemed to rcciprOcate the kindly greeting. The companY of Swedes and Nor- wegians numbered about 30 men; with nine women and about a dozen children. The object of the applause with which they were greeted was soon evident by an effort being made by many of the bottle hands to numb off a number of the foreigners to the Eagle and Child beerhonse, Church-street, the head-quarters of the workmen. They succeeded in taking about eight of the men there, but the remainder were marched off to the "Swe- dish barracks " in Corporation•st, where they were housed 1 under the direction of Messrs. Lyon. Some of the firm, 1 with two constables, afterwards visited the Eagle an Child, ' and after some difficulty persuaded the Swedes there to pro- ceed with them to the rest of the "colony." Daring the evening a large crowd gathered in Church-street, and the various phases of the subject were eagerly discussed. On Thursday at noon a deputation of the discharged workmen waited upon the directors of the firm with the view of amicably as tling the dispute, and arranging for the re- turn of the foreigners, but ne arrangement was come to. Later in the day a crowded toweling e the men was MU at the Eagle and Child, and Mr. James Hunter, who presided, warmly congratulated the discharged workmen on their be- haviour in not committing a breach of the peace on the arrival of the foreigners. Letters were read from the Dub- lin district and the Liverpool Trades Council, wishing the St. Helens committee every success in their efforts to induce the foreigners to leave the country.
For all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley and Wright's cotton is tbe beet.—Advt.

There have been two Cabinet meetings daring the week— one on Saturday and another on Wednesday. HIGH RAILWAY CHLHGES.—It was stated on Wednesday at a conference of representatives of the sea fishing industry that the railway companies we? e the cause of thousands of tons of fish being thrown overboard annually or used as manure. The carriage rate charged by the companies WAS, it was said, no less than 40 per cent on the gross pro- ceeds.

THE OLDHAM POISONING CASE —The Home Secretary has granted an order for the exhumation of the body of a Mrs Finley, mother of the Mrs Berry who has been com- mitted for trial on a charge of poisoning her daughter at the Oldham Workhouse. Mrs Finley died suddenly a year ago, and the police, in view of the cther charge against Mrs Berry, have been closely irquiring into the circumstances of her mother's death, of whose remains an examination will be made.

LORD HARTIRGTON AT NEWCASTLE.—Lord Hartincton, speaking at Newcastle, on lVemesdav night, said the duty of Liberal Unionists was to continue their sacrifices for. the object of maintaining the legislative union be!wern Great Britain and Ireland. There was at present a virtual coali- tion between the Consersative party and the Liberal Unionist party in the House of Commons without a coali- tion in the Government. He thought it wig better that there should be this independent support, but quite approved of the reasons which induced Mr. Goscben to join the Government. He did not admit that the great body of ,the Liberal party were irretrievably committed to the policy of the late Government, but believed that the more that policy was discussed the more doubt would be cast upon it. The recent criticisms of Lord Randolph Churchill would not make the slightest difference in the relations between the Liberal Unionists and the Conservatives. With regard to the negotiations for the re-union of the Liberal party, he need not say how thankful he would be if a national settlement of Irish questions could be arrived at. The negotiations might be safely left to Mr. Chamberlain and Bic George Trevelyan, but for himself he thought he would be doing better service by remaining outside, and keeping watch and guard. "Judge," said a young lawyer to a very successful settler," tell me the secret of your uniform success at the bar."
"Ab, young man, thtt secret is a life study, bat I wilt give it to you on condition that you pay all my bills durin this session of court."

"Agreed," said the junior. "Evidence, indisputable-evidence." At the end of the month the judge reminded the young man of his promise. "I recall no such promise." " Ah, but you made it." Your evidence, please." And the judge, not having any witnesses, lost a case for once.

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITIES.
div.p: SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITIES.

- - - --- Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held inquests at the Merton Bank Vaults, Park-road, on Monday, an the bodies of Charles Austin, aged 52 years, Park-road, and William Rigby, 21 years, Morley-street, who were killed at Messrs Piikington's collieries on the Thursday and Friday previous. Mr. Hall, Govern- ment Inspector, was present ; and Mr. John Swiftl solicitor, represented the Collieries Company. Mr. France, certificated manager, was also present. Austin, with his son John, was 1,000 yards from the shaft, building a pack, when a stone slipped between two bars and killed him. if the pack had been finished it would have supported the stone which fell. It was stated that the place was properly timbered, but in reply to questions a witness stated that they bad to ask the banksman for timber, not having a recqznised place where they could go for timber when they liked. Mr. Hall thought this simply an acci- dent, but added that he had corns to the conclusion that the supply of timber in this part of Lancashire was most nn- I satisfactory, and was one of the reasons that more people were silted by falls of roofs in this district than in any other pait of the United Kingdom.—The Coroner said from hie short experience he could concur in Mr. Hall's remarks. —Mr. France said messes. Pilkington's timber account amounted to £4,000 a year, and they provided a good sup- ply.—The Coroner said the remarks were not a reflection upon Messrs. Pilkington'a management, but were made generally of the district. A verdict of "Accidental death was returned.—ln the case of Rigby. who had fallen from a high-level tram line a distance of 25ft., a 3in, plank hav- ing broken when be came in violent contact with it, the coroner suggested, and the company promised, to pat a second bar;in the railint. A verdict of Accidental death" was returned. Mcßrighonse then proceeded to Rainford and held an inquest on the body of James Roden, forty-four years of age, of Barton's road, Rainford, who was killed in the Rushy Park Mine, belonging to . the Victoria Colliery Company, on Saturday. Roden went to his work in the morning as usual, but, as he did not re- turn in the afternoon, his wife went to the colliery to in- geire for him. A search was made in his working place, and the dead yody found under a stone weighing half a ton, which had fallen upon his head and chest from the roof. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
RHYMES! IN THE DIALECT. FOOAK AS, GMT) UP TO A BELL.

Wod tewin' an' drivin' an' humbug there is, An' o just for three meals a day! An' th' workin'-mon's life like a wet squib gooas "fiz," For wi' th' friction it's soon worn away. Wodever his job is— Plain weyvin' or dobbies— It's a fact, as aW know hi misel ; There's allus sum bother O'er summat or other For th' chap as geds up to a bell! Afooar five i' th' mornin', feaw "buzzers" him leawd, An' wakken up oat's i' bed; Then whistles an bells din an' jingle, while th' creawd 0' poor toylers, hard-tewd an' ill-fed, • Fey! on in a splutter, • O'er rooadway an' gutter, An' dash into th' fact'ry pell-melL They knots, if they're late in, Ther's eossing or bating For fooak as ged up to a bell. Then off !—hey, lads, hey! a stiff feight for a crust, Wi' t' weft bad, an' twist rotten stuff; While th' tackler, wi' temper an voyce booath artist, sweear yo're nod doin enuff ! Yor back wi gay heydin, Feels like yo'd bin kneydin For twenty-four heawrs ara spell! Ther's no "rest for t' weary," Life's dismal an dreary For th' fooak as ged up to a bell! Ther's sum noisy tyrants, ut's like mangy curs, They'n hearts 's as soft as gravestooans I ut They'll bully, an scowl, an' throw eawt nasty slurs, An' try to work th' flesh off yor booans, They're allus on 't grumble. They'll rooar an' they'll rumble •Thro't shop as they mek i' a hell! They're allus uncivil, An' playin the devil WI fooak as get up to a bell! Eleaw often id happens, wi' sickness i'th' heawse, A poor fella misses his rest, An' he pikes off to wark, wi' a heart like a meawse, Pitter-pattering fast in his breast. 0' two looms he's " whelpin', " ' An' yet ther's no helpin' Tho' he's slavin' for mooar than Inssel; • An' he's thin as a herrin', Wi't trouble he's bearin', An' shivers at th' seawnd ov a bell. It's a tussle, wi' muscle an' eye-sect an' brain, To mek a bare livin' wi' toy!; An' men as hey famlies to slave mun be fain Or else—o' ther stummicks ull spoyl! If%yo'd taste Life's honey, Dornd swap strength for money, Bud start as a gaffer yo'rsel'. An' when yo've nailt' treashur, Yo'll find eawt true pleashur, An' nod need to rise to a bell.

LIBERALS and Liberal Unionists will soon have very little to quarrel about if Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN is to be regarded as the typical Liberal Unionist. The platform of difference has never been so wide as art Tories sup- posed, and as they have tried to make it, and as things go it will soon be so narrow that there will not be as much as a plank left. The chief bone of contention amongst Liberals has always been understood to be whether the interpretation to be put upon Home Rule should be that Ireland should have a Parlia- ment of her own. Various schemes of local self-government, which involved nothing be- yond the administration of the law, have been spoken of by Liberal Unionists as their idea of Home Rule; but they were unacceptable because they did not go the full length of what is included in the word Parliament. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has always expressed himself as being favourable to the principle of Home Rule; but he has not until the last few days gone the length of admitting that he was ready to concede a Home Rule Parliament for Ireland. He has now reached this point, and we gladly welcome it as part of what, we trust, will be the happy outcome of the Round Table Conference. Speaking at Birmingham on Saturday evening, and referring to what should be done for the Irish people, he said "You must allow them to organize some form of fsovernment. What the exact form of government is to be is a matter which in my judgment concerns them much more than it does us. I should think that if they were anxious to be economical and business-like that they would have as little red tape and form as possible, that they would be satisfied with a standing committee, with a council and per- manent officers of some kind or other; but if they thought that they could be better served by imita- ting the cumberous forms of our Parliamentary gavernment, if they desire to have a Ministry, a Prime Minister, and a Minister of Agriculture and a Minister of Public Works, a Minister of Education, and a Cabinet; and to imitate on a small scale everything that goes on at Westminster, and in Parliament-street, and in Whitehall, all I can say again is that it seems to be a matter entirely for their discretion, and, with which I at all events have no desire whatever to interfere." It will be noted that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN does not use the word Padiament ; but what of that? • He describes a Parliament; and a rose by any other name smells just as sweet. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL recognises the extraordinary step forward which the member for West Birmingham has made, and, as it leaves his tordship, , for the present, stranded, he is not a little un- easy. Speaking in the debate on the Address on Monday evening, he said he thought Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was pursuing an erroneous and mistaken, eonrset "N 9 P'11111;er,1 he I added, "on this side, so far as I know, will ever follow him in the line of policy which, by any reasonable construction, could create in Dublin anything of the nature of an Irish Parliament." It is of little moment, com- paratively, that the Tories are not in favour of a Home Rule Parliament; but it is of moment to know that some Liberal 'Jnionists have advanced so far, for it is a matter of course to say that when Lord RARTIRGTON and his friends also move forward the SALISBURY Government will go to the wall. And no one is aware of this better than Lord RANDOLPH. He spoke of the present Tory alliance with the Liberal Unionists as "a useful kind of crutch," but he warned his friends against attaching too much importance to "precarious Parliamentary/ alliances, which are transient and uncertain as the shifting wind." His lordship is evidently pretty wide awake as to what is coming; he sees the beginning of the end. We do not wish it to be supposed that the difficulties of the Liberal party ire over— far from that. There is a great deal to 'do in the way of determining conflicting issues even when the principle has been accepted, all round, that Ireland shall be allowed to have a Parliament of her own. We quite agre..,. with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in saying that "no scheme will have a real , chance of success which is not the joint pro• , duction of many minds, which is not built up by the contributions of different persons approaohing the qmestion from many differ- ent points of view." Concession on one side must be met by concession on the other, and we are confident, now that the member for West Birmingham can, without ambiguity, be described as a Home Ruler, that Mr. GLAD- STONE will not show himself a stickler as to : matters of minor importance. Mr. CHAM- , BERLION seems to think that the stumbling ' block in the way of a settlement is a dis- position on the part of the Irish tleaders to dictate terms. We do not ourselves anticipate } a difficulty of this kind, remembering as we I do that the Home Rule scheme was not formulated by Mr. PARNELL, hat vas rather accepted by him when presented to the House of Commons and to the country by Mr. GLADSTONE. There has been a good' deal of hard hitting on all sides; and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has struck out ao hard as anyone; but we shall have to confess our- selves much mistaken if, ere long, there is not an end of this cross,. firing. Liberals and Liberal Unionists and Irish Nationalists, have expended a deal of ammunition on each other—much to their detritno.nt and to the delight of the Tories. It is time for a change; they must make up the:r quarrel, and save their powder and shot for the enemy.

CHARACTER is of tha greatest value in our I public men, and Warrington has sustained a great loss by the death of Mr. CHARLES BROADBENT who meras a public man of the highest character. To know him was to es- 'll teem him, for he was a gentleman in the best 0,1 sense of that much-abused word. As Mayor, Magistrate, Town Councillor, and Goat dian of the poor—posts which amongst ethers he filled--he showed that it was possible to com- bine the strictest interest in the public wel- fare with the kindest -regard for his fellow- townsmen. No one ever approached him either on publjc or private business, and found him other than courteous and consi- derate. Staunch and true to his principles as a Liberal, he could hold his own svith a tenderness and a grace which often, by contrast, put to shame the rowdiness of the mare vulgar politician. It is this feature in his character which caused him to • be welcome' wherever he went—in Conser- vative as well as in Liberal circles ; and it will keep his memory green in the years that are to come. There is much, doubtless, that is formal and customary in public expressions of condolence, but no one can peruse those that have been uttered in connection with the death of slr. BROADBENT without feeling that they are the outcome of genuine regard for a genuine man. To the famPy, who are weighed down with a sense of the irre- parable loss they also have sustained, votes of condolence will present themselves for the moment as empty offerings, but the time vill come when something of consolation will be found in the knowledge that the hus- band and father who has passed away ditl his duty in life faithfully and weli, and was revered by his fellow citizens alike for his

The Glass Bottle-makers of St. Helens are out on strike against the introduction of foreign workmen; and " the sound of battle hurtles in the air," or, as the "P.D.," murdering Shake.spere, once got it—" the sound of bottles hustles in the air."

The Guardians of Warrington and of Run- corn (along with other authorities) have been asked to go round with the hat on behalf of the Imperial Institute; but they " don't see it." They are overflowingly loyal of course;. but their loyalty doesn't gush over in this particular direction. They grew quite mirth- ful over the Prince of Wales's call to "stump up." One member, in the true Parliament- ary fashion, suggested that the matter might be adjourned to that day six months. He has evidently no hope of a knighthood, or even of a bust. He was of opinion that anything done with regard to the Qaeen's Jubilee should be done locally, and so thought others. The Guardians rightly conclude that charity as to individuals and as to institutes should begin at home. - „

They say that at the Warrington Conser- vative Ball, on Thursday night, matters at one time grew " fast and furious; " that there was a lively bout of fisticuffs ; that " ruddy•gore " presented itself; and that sundry dress suits have been hurt 'past all surgery." No wonder whilst all this was go- ing on "the lights in the chamber burned blue." But—`• mum 's the word."

-- Mr. Robert Pierpoint, as the "Young Obediah " who is understood to be waiting for the shoes of the "Old Obediah," was the s'pokesman at the Warrington Conservative Club on Monday. He had a fling at the Irish members of Parliament, remarking that "many of them had emerged from the ob- scurity which would otherwise have hidden them for ever." In this respect they have at least an advantage over Mr. Pierpoisi.—he has not yet " ernergedY

Pkrpoint had a fling, too, at Perfec- tion Soap; but he had nothing to say as to Ale which is not Perfection. Perhaps it did not occur to him to remark that Soap is sug- gestive of cleanliness, and that "cleanliness is next to Godliness ;" while Ale is sugges- tive of dirt, disease, death, and another " d— " which shall be nameless.

Mr. Goschen is like the Wandering Jew, or like Noah's dove—a prettier simile—for he finds no rest for the sole of his foot. He was late of Edinburgh, later of Liverpool, and now he has left the Masses to join the Classes in St. George's, Hanover Square. He sticks to his text; he is "determined to up- hold the Union." It is very good of him; if he cannot be a prop (or shall we say a "crutch") inside, he may, in his way, uphold the Union as an outsider—say, as a "flying buttress."

It must 'be galling to the "crippled" Go- vernment to be reminded by Lord Randolph Churchill that their reliance is on "the Unionist crutch." In this case "the crutch" —reversing the usual order of things—has so muth control over "the cripple" that a line might, fittingly, be added to an old couplet— thus _ _ _
In matters commercial the fault of the Dutch Is giving too little and taking too much; [And. 'tis also the fault of the Unionist r.ittelt].

It was a happy thought of the Warring- ton magistrates to bind over two young soldiers who had been fighting, each in his own recognisa.nces for the other's behaviour. Henceforward each will be interested in the other keening the peace; but if the peace should go to pieces—if they should take to Eghting each other again—they will be the means of inticting a heavy cite upon them- selves. This is as it should be.

Pity the poor Czar! When he drives out he is protected by a corps of scouts, some seven hundred strong, who are stationed at various places on the route. The divine William spoke like a seer when he said— 'Uneasy lies the head that wears a cvown." The Czar would he better with another "crown "--with five shillings in his pocket, and freedom. He would have a 'ighter purse, but what of that .? He would have a lighter heart.

The United States Government are .bout to do their duty by Walt Wtitman in rranting him a pension of twenty.fse dollars a•month. He did great service, and well nigh ruined his health, in hospital work during the Civil War. And then, has he not sung in this own quaint way the song of the American Democ- racy ? Come,S•will make the continent indisstluble, I will make the most splentiid race theA. tin ever
shone upon, I will make divine magnetic !lands, With the love of comrades, With:the life-long love of comrades.

Walt Whitman will not be ashamed to re- ceive aid in his old days. He can freely receive, 'because he has so freely given, He will say, as of yore 'What you,give me I ckeerfully accept, A little ,sustenance, -a hut and garden, a little money, as I rendezvous with my poecat, A traveller s lodging, and breakfast as I 'ourney throug'i the State.

Coming a little nearer home, who is there with Lancashire blood in h:s veins who is not delighted to see the honour done to Edwin Waugh by giving him a dinner on his Seven- tieth Birthday? Lte was snatched but re- cently from the jaws of death, and lie has sung so well since that it :iv to be hoz)ed he will charm the Man with •the Scythe into forgetfulness for irony years to come. lENTERTAINMENT AT WrieWEs.—An entertainment was on Thursday evening given by the members of the Nelson- street Band of Hope in the chapel. Mr. J. B. Hudson pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. An excellent pro- gramme of recitations, duets, songs, dialogues, &c., was gone through in a proiseworthv manner. SERVICE or SONG AT WIDNES —On Tuesday evening, in Hutchinson-strwr Primitive Methodist Chapel, tbe mem- bers of the Band of Hope, assisted by a few friends, gave an enjoyable renderiaz of the service of song " Nimble Nat." Mr. S. Owens occupied tti chair and delivered an appro.. priive address, and the narrative was capitally read by Mr. E. Carey. TRADESMEN'S BALL AT WIDNES. The second annual " Tradesmen's ball " was held in the Dubs Assembly Roorne, on Monday evening. There were about 50 Couples present, and Mr. E. Doyle officiated as M.O. Dancing was kept up until five o'clock next morning, to the strains of Mr. J. Gordon's band. Mrs Bray, of Victoria-road, supplied the refreshments,__

FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORES.—About six o'clock on Thursday evening the arch of one of furnaces in the Black Ash Department of Messrs. Hutchinson's works, collapsed. The flames she.- up to a great height, and set on fire a pitch pine high level bridge leading to a revolver. The fire was quickly subdued, and the damage done was only trifling in amount. LECTURE AT APPLETON.—Mr. H. Wade Deacon, of Ap- pleton, on Monday evening delivered his popular lecture on "Homes without hands" in St. Bede's schoolroom, Apple- ton. The Very Ray. Dean Finegan occupied the chair. The attractiveness of the lecture was greatly increased by
lime-light illustrations, which were directed by Mr'. Vero Charles Dritilelq. The proceeds were in aid of a ceme- tery wall.

VISIT OF A GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR TO RUNCORN.—On Tuesday, Dr. John Spear, one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board visited Runcorn for the purpose of making inquiries as to whether there were or had been any cases of fever within the limits of the district of the Runcorn Lnproventent Act, 1852, arising from destitution. It is pleasing to report that assurances were given to Dr. Spear to the effect that no such case existed or had been in existence in the district.

I - VAILERE OF WIDNES MAN —At the Liverpool Bank- ruptcy Caws, on Thursday, John Merrick, journeyman cooper, 42, Widnes-road, Widnes came rp on his public ex- amination. The statement of aff airs showed that the debtor, for whom Mr. Higher/1 appeared, was deficient to the extent of £167. Examined by the official receiver, the debtor stated that his wife had been carrying on a drapery ard millinery business, and his eister a furniture shop. In consequence of a prolonged illness in his family the shops had been neglected, and heavy expenses incurred. The examination was adjourned to the 10th inst. DAMAGING PLANTATIONS AT ALVA.NLEY.—At Eddisbury , Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Parker of Alvanley„ WAS charged with wilfully damaging timber, the property of the Marquis of Chehnondeley. Mr. Preston prosecuted. Jos.. Evans, farmer, Helsby, said that he had charge of the plan- tatiors on the estate of the Marquis of Cholua,maeley. On the 4th January, about 3 p.m., he was in one of the plant a- liens when ha heard the sound of an axe, lie went to see where it came from, and he found defendant autting timber and putting it in a heap to take away. Defendant was fined £2, inclediag costs. BRTNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS RENCDRN On Wednesday evening the members of the above debating society met to listen to a paper by Mr, John Hoffer(' on n The history and mystery of tonic sot-fa." The essayist gave a brief restzmc of the history of the tonic notation from the eleventh century, when Guido, a monk, applied ceetain signs to the musical scale, which, with little altera- tion, are the same as now in uee. MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances when they first find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- taoles which id the end datise their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, Manchester, and 143, Lord-street, Southport, has invented his "Perfection " Spectacles, which he adopts at either of the above addresses at 7a 6d per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness • coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight " free on application.—Advt. TILE CONSECRATION'Or ST. PAUL'S CRORCR, WIDNES.— The consecration services were continued on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, twice occupied the pulpit, and preached to large congregations. The collections in aid of the fund for providing a much needed parochial room amounted to the total sum of La. A FLAT SUNK AT WIDNES.—The flats Martha and Earl of Derby, belonging to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, of Sankey Bridges, and laden with sand, were making for Widnes Dock on Satarday afternoon, when they came in collision. The Martha was badly damaged on the starboard quarter, filled with water and quickly sank. The captain (Samuel Holden) and two harms rowed ashored in the small boat. The ether vessel, of which Joseph Rotheram is captain, was Rot much damag.d.

WIDNES NATIONALIST LEAGI7E —A concert was held under the auspices of the Widnes Branch of the Irish League on Monday evening. The room was densely crowded; the concert was of a very enjoyable character, and was much appreciated. In the interval, an address was delivered by Mr. Madden, solicitor, of Liverpool, on the Irish question. He spoke forcibly and eloquently on the subject for about half an hour, and was frequently loudly applauded. The entertainment passed off in a most agree- able manner.

The annual meeting of the members of this association was held in the reading-room, High-street, on Monday even- ing. Attention was drawn to the fact that owing to the lukewarmuess of the membera, and a want of intereston the part of the public the Bible Class, and the Historical Class had had to be abandoned, „ and that the membership had fallen from 11l to 53. While had not the library been sold, the accounts for the year would have shown a considerable deficit. These facts showed that the association was in a critical period of its career, and retrenchment ard reform there must of necessity Le during the coming year. APPALLING DISASTERS AT SEA. A BRITISH EMIGRANT STEAMER SUNK.— OVER 200 LIVES LOST. On Monday the following telegrams were received The Australian emigrant ship Kapunda has been run down off the coast of Brazil by an unknown steamer. It is feared that over 200 lives have been lost. The Kapunda was an iron ship of 1,095 tons. She left England in Dec- ember bound to Fremantle, Western Australia. The steamship which ran down the Kapunda is believed to have been a French vessel. Her name has not been ascertained. Some of the crew of the Kapunda have reached the coast, and it is from them that news of the disaster has been received. The loss of life, it is feared, is even greater than the 200 first stated. The passengers, it is understood, were all Government emigrants, who had received assisted passages. The Kapunda was built in 1875 by Messrs. McMillan and Sons, of Dumbarton and is owned by Messrs. Trinder, Anderson. and Co.. London. On Tuesday morning the following details were to hand :—The Kapunda sailect on Dec. 11 from London for Freemantle, Western Australia. She called at Plymouth on December 18, and had on board four cabin passengers, two hundred and sixty-eight steerage passengers, and 40 hands to work the vessel. Captain John Masson, the master, had been in the service of the owners several years. The vessel took a cargo of about 600 tons of general goods, and had 300 tons of stone ballast. She was lightly laden, drawing only 15ft. 2in. When she left dock she was under the full operation of the Pas- senger Act, and subject to the regulations of the Board of Trade. The vessel had on several previous occa- sions carried passengers to Australia. Messrs. LOSS OF A CfIAISNEI:MAIL STEAMER.-EXCITING
SCENE

The Weymouth and Channel Islands Company's steamer Brighton, Captain Painter, was totally wrecked off tee Guernsey coast on Saturday morning. The Brighton, which is a paddle steamer and the beet of the company's fleet, left Weymouth at midnight on Friday, but she was only able to proceed at half epePd owing to the dense fog prevailing. Her whistle was kept blowing at regular inter- vals throughout the night. The speed was further slackened on nearing ths Guernsey coast, and it was while the boat was proceeding dead slow that she suddenly struck violently upon cue of the treacherous rocks that abound upon the coast. The captain immediately ordered the engines to be reversed, and the vessel floated off, but the bows were com- pletely stove in, and the water rushed into the doomed ves- sel in one west volume. The time at which the vessel struck was ten minutes to seven, and nearly all the paisenrers were then in their berths. Such of them as had not been roused by the shock were now hurriedly called on deck, and told off to the respective boats. Fortunately the sea was comparatively calm. The boats ware speedily lowered, and the whole of the 25 passengers rapidly took their places without any confusion or much apparent excitement. The crew and firemen, numbering 23, also took their places in the boat. Captain Painter being the last to leave the ship. Indeed, it was enly at the earnest solicitation of the pas- sengers that the captain at length left his vessel. The °oat load only just put off when the Brighton gave one or two ominous heaves. Her stern went high into the air and she plunged down, head foremost, the boats only being just clear of the suction caused by the sinking ship. The mails went down with tbe vessel, and nearly all the passengers' baggage was also lost. It is believed the vessel lies in 15 fathoms of water, and there is a possibility that the mails may be saved.

Mr. Mann' Bowswrs then read Ilse letter, which was ad- dressed to Mrs. Broadbent, and said :—*Dear Madam,—The members of the General Council of thy Warrington Liberal Association desire to express their deep and sincere regret at the death of Mr. Broadbent, and at the tame time to Place upon record their high appreciation of the great services rendered by him during an active and meat useful life, not merely to the cause of Liberalism, bat to all movements of a philanthropic aed nseful character connected with this town and neighbourhood. We desire to assrxe von also of the heartfelt sympathy we all feel for yourself and family in this your sad bereavement." The CHAIH/dAN then proposed that the letter lie gent from the Association to Mrs. Broadbent.

Mr. F. 51011K9-seC;;l:cF;l7;;:oposition. He did it, he Mid, with feelings of regret, because for a great many years he was thrown very intimately into connection with Mr. Broadbent as a matter of business. As many of them would know, it was mainly owing to Mr. Porter and Mr. Broadhent that they were able to start White Cross. They had also been thrown together in chapel matters, so that be knew, perhaps as well as most, something of the value of Mr. Broadbent, and something of the principles that actuated him in his course through life. He entirely endorsed what Mr. MoMinnies bad said, and he was quite sure that the meeting would sympathise most deeply with Mrs. Broil& bent in her loss, and also with Miss Harvey, one of the most beautiful characters they had ire Warrington,because she had been to the whole family mere like a mother.

Mr. Wri.max PIERPOrNT, who supported the resolution, said that his earliest associations in life were connected with their dear old friend of Latchford. He did not think that in the thirty years acquaintance he had bad with Mr. Broadbent that ever a wrong word had passed between them. He did not think that any words of praise could be too highly strung in speaking of the memory of Mr. Charles Broadbent, chairman of the Lacbford Ward Committee. It was mainly due to Mr. Broadbent that he (Mr. Pierpoint) ventured to take any step towards active political life, and he was encouraged by Mr. Broadbent to go on labouring in the field of Liberal politics. He could say a great deal in favour of Mr. Broadbent, but it would be unnecessary. He should, however, like to testify on behalf of the Latchford Ward Committee, that they felt highly gratified that the Association had taken upon itself the drawing up of that letter of condolence.

Mr. T. BIIICHALL said that he had also had a long in- timacy with Mr. Broadbent. For thirty-dye years he had known him, and he did not remember a cross or aegry word ever baying passed between them. After having worked with Mr. Broadbent in religious matters, and in other ways, his feeling at Mr Broadbent's death was something like what must be felt by soldiers campaigning when an old comrade had fallen by the way. He was glad that oppor- tunity had been taken by the meeting to bear testimony to Mr. Broadbent' worth, and to condole with his wife .and family. The resolution was then carried. r

At the conclusion of the morning sermon in Cairo-street Chapel, on Sunday morning, the organist (Mr. Gray) played the "Dead March" in "Saul," and, after tho Bene- diction had been pronounced, and the scholars had dis- persed, a meeting was held, the Rev. R. Filcher presiding. —Mr. MDLLARD (secretary) said he was sure there was nut a member of the congregation who did not feel that he or she had received a heavy blow in the lamented loss of one ef its noblest members in the person of Mr. Broadbent, and it was for the object of passing a resolution of sympathy and condolence with the bereaved widow and family that he had asked them to remain after the service. The resolu- tion read as follows :—'That this, a special meeting of the congregation worshipping at Cairo-street Chapel,. desires to express its deep sympathy and condolence with Mrs. Broad- bent and family in their bereavement through the lamented death ut Mr. Broadbent ; and, further, desires to place on record the great loss the congregation has sustained of one who for many years rendered most valuable services i and , that the memory of hint will long be cherished in the affect. , Lion of both chapel and school. Also that the Secretary be requested to forward a copy of the resolution to Mrs. Broad- bent."—Mr. F. Motes moved the resolution.—Mr. W. D. HOCIGHTON, in secon4ing the motion, raid he was sure they all felt the great void which had occurred by the death of their friend, and the severance of his long, useful, and in- timate connection with the congregation—bin life-long connection would be felt by all of them. It behoved them to take upon themselves the increased responsibility, and to imitate what was truest and best in their friend'S character. —The resolution was unanimously carried, all standing, at the request of the Chairman.—At a special meeting of the teachers of the school, held on Sunday afternoon, the Rev. B. Pitcher in the chair, the following resolution was car- ried, on the motion el Mr. Thomas BIRCPEALL, seconded by Mr. W. H. 'Flumes (superintendent) :—" That the Secre- tary be requested to convey to Mrs. Broadbent and the members of her family the deep sympathy of their teachers in their cad bereavement, and to express the great sorrow the teachers have felt in bearing of the death of Mr. Broadbent, who had at all times been ready to assist the teachers in the carrying oat of the work of the school insti- tution."

div.p: AT THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

At the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Com- merce, on Monday, Mr. F. MONKS, the president, proposed that a vote of condolence with Mrs. Broadbent on the occa- sion of the death of her husband, who had been not only a I member but president of the Chamber, be passed.—Mr. JOYEPif DAVIES soconded the motion, and remarked that they felt for Mrs. Broadbent in the loss of her husband, who had been a most estimable man, apart from his public life. Ile had acted with uniform courtesy, even more than most of them; and he never said an unkind word to or of any one. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JOLLEY said that he had met Mr. Broadbent for many years as a member of the Town Council, as a Guardian, and at the Savings' Bonk, Infirmary, and other institutions. and his conduct bad been all that could be desired. He was a gentleman in every sense of the word. —Mr. Cansorr said that having been closely connectrd in business with Mr. Broadbent for some years past, he should be sorry not to add his testimony to the loss which be con- sidered the community had sustained, AS well as the irre- parable loss which Mm. Broadbent and her family would also sustain, by the death of one who was a most affec- tionate, considerate, and kind father and husband. Refer- ence bad been made to the deceased's public life, as a coun- cillor, magistrate, member of the Chamber of Commerce and as a guardian. All these offices, so far as he, as one of the public coulA judge, were filled with the utmost satisfac- tion to the town. He corroborated what Mr. Davies had said. He had never beard Mr. Broadbent, during a seven years' intimacy, utter a word to the detriment of any burial). , being; jilt wen in his power to do a kindly action he al- ways did it. Judging of Mr. Broadbent from what he hag known of him intimately with regard to business relationsv his simplicity of character and, his strict integrity were two features which could not fail to strike anyone. He should personally reel his loss very much.—The resolution wash then carried.
AT THE LITERARY_ AND PHILOSOPHICAL
SOCIETY.

At a meeting of this society, of which the deceased gentleman was a member, held on Tuesday evening, the chairman, Mr. T. G. RYLANDS, said that he could not help feeling that there was one subject that he sbould introduce and it wee one upon which he should have no need to claim an expression of their sympathy; he referred to the death of Mr. Broadbent. Most of them would remember that Mr. Broadbent had filled the office of president of that society, that he had acted as secretvy, and that no member had been more regular in his attendance, or more willing to assist them in every possible way. They would all miss him. There was about him a genial kindness which was like sunshine. He thought that they should take some Course, de a society, to express to Mrs Broadbent and her family the strong feelings of sympathy they entertained.— Mr. Bataistcnax said that he was sure the large assembly met there would heartily coincide with what the chairman had said. He greatly deplored the loss of Mr. Broadbent, and was very sorry that they should see him no more amongst I them, but they mot not neglect to express to his surviving widow and family the dew sympathy they felt with them In theft sudden bereavement. They all lamented that be- reavement, and should long remember how many services he was ready to give when they were required of him. He moved—" That the members of this society hereby express to Mrs Broadbent and her family their deep Sym- pathy with them id their bereavement, and, record their sensa of the great loss Mr. Mroadhent's death will oc- casion, not only to the society, but to the whole community ii which his active and useful life was passed."—Mr. ROBERT DAVIES seconded the proposition. It had; he re- marked, been well said by one of old times that "concerning the dead nothing but good is spoken," but be had no diffi- culty in this case, as he felt sure that the eulogiuMs that had been passed upon his memory by the president and by Mr. Beamont, were felt by them all to be well indeed de- served. Although as a society they had nothing to do with his public life they could not forget he gave to them an excellent example as a goad father of a family, and a good I Citizen fulfilling the municipal offices of his native town.— The motion having been carried the ordinary business of the meeting„was proceeded with.

THE FUNERAL. The mortal remains of the late Mr. Broadbent were interred on Thursday in the shurchvard at Grappenhall, near to the grave of his eldest dongh- ter, Miss Alice Lydia, who died on the 2811* of October, 1883. Respect for the memory of the de- ceased gentleman was shown in Latchford and Grappenboll by the drawing of blinds, and the putting up of shutters, and at the graveside there gathered a large number of friends, and many others who wiehed to pey a last tributecto the memory of a respected fellow-townsman. A little before twelve o'clock, the funeral procession, which was com- priasd of the hearse and twenty-eight mourning coaches: left the late residence of the deceased, and proceededon its mournful journey. The carriages were principally occu- pied by relatives and personal friends of the family, but a few were empty, and were sent as a mark of respect by their owners. Amongst them was thattof Councillor Platt,. who was unable to be present. The peocession was wit- nessed by a considerable number. of people. The church was reached at a quarter past twelve, and a solemn service was held in the church. The The Rev Canon .Greenall, rector of Grappenhall, and the• Rev R B Prescott, vicar of Chrlit Church., Latchford, read. the order for the burial of the dead. The hymn commenc- ing, "For ever with the Lord," was afterwards sung. Canon Greenall and the Rev B B Prescott officiated at the grave. The coffin, which was of fumed oak, panelled, with silver mountings, was literally covered with beautiful wreaths. Many of the mourners also carried wreaths. An engraved sheet plate on the coffin bore the following inscription : " Charles Broadbent, born 31st July, 1830, died January 29th, 1887." Messrs Robert Garnett and Sons, of Sankey- street, were the undertakers. GR.LMMAR SCHOOL V. OLD BOYS —This match was played in Arpley on Saturdly, and resulted in a win for the school by two goals and four tries to one try. The Old Boys had a strong team, but were beaten at all points of the game. For the winners Brundrett, &Awn, and Williamson, jun.' played well, as did Henry, Horton, and Evans for the Old Boys. FRIENDS' qCIIOOL, FEERETH, V. COWLEY dRAMNAR SCHOOLS, ST. HELENS —On Saturday this match was played at Penketh, and resulted in favour of the Penketh slab by &goals to nil. Simpson (forward) did good service for the home team by scoring five goals. Gumersall and Smith also helped the score, the former by two and the latter one goal. Cowley Grammar School fought well, bat were in this instance over-matched. This is the seventh match for Penketh, who have won five, drawn two, and lost none this season.

WIDNES T. ToTrierGa•OL—Played at Widnes on Saturday, in the presence of about 2,000 spectators. The visitors came with .onlv thirteen men, but secured a substitute. They kicked off up the slope; and after some fast ,play, by which the borne quarters were entered, Harding ran to the Tottington line, passing most of his opponents in fine style, when he was tackled, and losing the ..ball' it Was touched down. A few minutes afterwards a pass to Worthington, who was directly in front of the Widnes citadel, enabled that pi Ayer to drop a splendid goal. This had the effect of rousing the energies of the home team, while rendering the visitors absurdly careful, as they several times touched down when there was not the slightest need. Widnes con- tinued to have the upper band, several times having "hard lines," until at the middle of the second half Howard, by good play, secured a try. The place was difficult, and though Morris kicked well he did not land a goal. Several other misors were addtd by Widnes, and at the close t4e score stood—Tottington one goal and one minor to Widnes one try and six minors. For Widnes, Bingham, Harding, Farrell, Howard, Keddie, Smith, Fogg, and Pervin were frequently conspicuous. and Coop and Worthington played a line game for Tottington. WARRINGTON T. ROCHDALE HORNETS (A Taams.)— On Saturday the Warrington "A " team balanced the defeat they sustained at Rochdale on the 27th November, by de- cisivelv defeating the then victors, Rochdale " A " team. -Rochdale won thstOste, and Whittle kicked off at 3-15, a poor return being made, the ball going into touch near the centre. Soon after the commencement Walsh got a severe kick on the ankle, which compelled him to retire from the field, Warren appearing later on as a substitute. Whittle next gave the ball to Nevins, who transferred to Boardman. The lattei- player; on being tackled, passed to the forwards, who failed to avail themselves' of, the opportunity thus afforded. 'Antrobtie came round the scrimmage with the oval, but was brought doigif by Barton. Whittle passed to Nevins, who kicked finely late touch Craghan now made a geed dribble, and Nevins oollared Thorpe before he could get the ball away. Wylde, Jackson. and Nuttall took play to centre, where Molyneaux, Eyes, and Adamson came through the scrimmage and dribbled to the visitors' 25 Some good passing between Whittle, Nevins, and Boardman almost resulted in the,latter player scoring; he only being' stopped by Holmes a few yards from the line. • Parkinson, Bradley. and Wylde came away with a grand dribble, their progress being stopped by Unsworth kicking into touch. Barton and Pennington pressed on, taking the ball to the Warrington line, Unliworth having to save by touching down. Ashursr dropped out, and the ball eventually went Into torch. Hackett got possession from the line out, and made a dash dbwn the field, being stopped by Pennington. Some kicking between Boardman and Pennington now took place, and Molyneaux and Ashram, by a good dribble, took play to centre, Smith saving firmly. Jones and Eyes were next conspicuous, and Dillon, Cragban, and Unsworth fur- ther improved matters by taking the oval to. the visitors' 25. Warren a few minutes previous to this came on the field, and took Walsh's place at centre three•quarter, Uns- worth going in the forwards again; the home team having played 14 men for about twenty minutes. Whittle now gave the oval to Warren, who transferred to Boardman, the latter kicking to Pennington, who put \ in a fine punt, Jolley responding with one equally as good. Barton now got the ball awayfrom the scrimmage and passed to Smith, who kicked, and follcwing well up collared Jolley before he could part with the ball. half-time was now called, with the score Rochdale -Hornets. 1 minor • trar- rington, nil. On resuming, ?fatten kicked off for li,:acbdale, Molyneaux charging the kick down, the ball eventually go- ing intotouch. Cragban, Dillon, Ashurst, and Jones took play to the Hornets' 25, and Whittle getting hold, passed to Warren, who in turn gave the oral to Boardman, Pen- nington bringing him down. Thorpe now put in a good kick, and Jolley, with a fine punt, sent the ball near the visitors' line, where from a scrimmage E. Dillon succeeded in getting a try, Ashurat's kick being a failure. Nuttall dropped out and Antrobus put in a short run and passed to warren, who was collared by Smith. Nevins here made his mark and gained a lot of ground by a free kick. ntrobus next got in a good run and passed to Boardman, who pun- ted down the field, Nevins kicking the ball touch in goal. Adamson returned the drop oat, and Eyes, Dillon, Moly- neaux, and Jones made a good dribble, Thorpe having to save by kicking dead. Wylde dropped out, Jolley returning with a huge punt, the oval resting in the Rochdale 25. Schofield, Parkinson, and Nuttall worked Mihail to centre, Iwhere Antrobus passed to Warren, who was collared by

Smith. Whittle now mad* a splendid dribble, Thorpe stop- ping his progrees near the Roe, a touchdown being regis- tered immediately afterward:a. Some good passing between Arttrobur, Whittle, Warren, and Boardman caused pliy to be located near the Rochdale goal-line, but Pitting relieved to quarter flag. Antrohns next got hold and put in a good run, being collared close to the line, the visitors touching down in self defence. Immediately after tbe drop oat Whittle passed to Warren, who re-parsed to Boardman, this payer dropping a beautifd goal amid great applause. Smith restarted from the centre, and the vis-itors took '3/ay to the home 25. Racket,, however, relieved by a good run, and Smith next gaining pomessien kicked into touch. Whittle agairgave the ball to Warren, who threw across to Board- man, and the latter pot in a nine run, Pennington bringing him down. ahertly afterward* time was called, leaving Warrington victorious by 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 mincrrs to Rochdale 1 minor. Rochdale Hornets o Full back, Thorpe; three-quarter backs. SmitkPennington, and Hol- man; half backs, Pilling and Barton ; forwards, G. H. Nattall (captain), Bradley, Parkinson, Wylde, Schofield, Hastings, Ashworth, Jaekson, and Forseer. WARRTNGTOff 'V. ROCHDALE HORNETS. On Saturday the return fixture between the Warrington and Rochdale Hornets team was brought off at R'ocbdale. The visitors were witbont Fair Turner, who on the same afternoon was playing with the Lancashire county team against Durham county at Manchester. On the other band the Hornets pat a strong force in the field, evidently with the intention if retrieving their former defeat at Warring- ton. The game was witnessed by about 2,000 spectator& H. Ashton won the toss, and Frank Turner kicked off, but the ball going out of play bad to be brought back again; theball bounding into touch from the next kick-off. Barnes first lead off with a nice rush and followed on with a good kiek, Buckley taking a Liking kick at the ball and returning it well up the field. Jolley next obtained a free kick for 1 offeide tackling, a good scrimmage taking place. A lot of scrambling play on the Hinneete part let them into the Warrington quarters, where some scrimmages took place. From the line-out the ball was not thrown out straight, but the Hornets rushed en and Wild obtained a try. This, of course, was objected to, the referee admitting that the ball .was not thrown out straight. Ashton, therefore, very wisely refused to charge the kick at goal, the matter being left to be decided by the Rugby Union. Smith just landed the goal from the place. Frank Turner kicked eff and then Speakman mat in a nice run and splendidly teckled Nuttall. Mellidew, Wild, and Smith next brohe away, but Gilbert proved one too maoy for them, and frustrated their efforts in taking the ball a great distance. Naftali next passed to Smith, who put in a nice kick, Appleton returning. Gilbert led off from the loose with a dribble, and then good screw scrimmaging was witnessed. The ball becomieg loose Dillon, Turner, Rigby, and Gilbert broke away. Frank Turner pickeci tip and transferred to Gilbert, who scored the first try for the cup holders. Although this was near touch Frank Turner landed a splendid goal. Barnes returned nicely after kick off, and then Wild, Rowe, and Mellidew took the oval back to 25. Jolley next intercepted a pass by Nolan to Hastings and got in a strong run, but Wild brought him down. A free kick wae next acceded to the visitors for off- side collaring, but nothing much came of it. Some good scrimmages were next witnessed, Massey twice in sue- cession tackling Smith. Beckley obtained a free kick fro.n one by Barnes and sent the ball to touch, Dillon, Frank Turner, and Heyes broke through and took play down the field, but Griffiths checked. Then Wild and Mellidew broke away and confined play to the visitors' 25. Mellidew next seemed like sowing, but Barnes and Gilbert brought him down. Frank Turner, Littlewood, and Ashton led from the pack, the first-named taking the ball past the 25. Wild next tried to get sway, but Jolley being on the alert stop- ped his progress, which brought about belt-time, with the score Warrington one goal one minor, Rochdale one goal (disputed.) Some- time elapsed before the ball was re- started, Ashton charging it down. Hayes got bold and caused a scrimmage to be formed in the centre. Smith re- ceived a pass from Nuttall, but Miseey checked him. Massey next received a free kick, Wild getting hold and making a nice run. Barnes returned a kick by Griffith; and • Has- tings came to grief, being tackled well by Jolley.. From a loose scrimmage Nolan took the oval up the field, and after a lot of furious play, Mellidew got over, Wild failing at goal. This put the cup holders en their mettle, and play was very determined ind fast. Hough got in a short run, followed by Griffiths trying to get away,being collared by Barnes. Nolan was now lucky in getting the ball, but Gilbert and Jolley were on the alert, and were too much for Nolan and Has- tings. For a few minutes the cup holders exhibited some of their old form, for Frank Turner got bold, passed to Dil- lon. Dillon to Rigby, Rigby to Frank Turner, who gave it to Gilbert, who scored the second try, Frank Turner making a good though ineffectual bid at goal. Nothing further was scored, the noticeable items being a good run and tackle by Jolley, good collaring by Speakman and Gilbert, a nice dribble by Littlewood, and good forward play, the game being drawn after 70 minutes play. Score: Warrington one goal one try and one minor, to one goal (disputed) and a try.

fho game was somewhat rough, especially on the Hornets' part, who evidently did not mean to lose, the spectators saying that a better gime has not been witnessed on the Rochdale ground. Both lots of forwards worked very hard, and at times the screw scrimmaging on both aides was a treat to witness, Warrington haying tho beet ot Davies, Ashton, Dillon, and Hayes worked bard in the pack. whilst none were more conspicuous than Frank Turner; Rigby also doing good work on the loose. The two half backs tackled surprisingly ; Gilbert also dribbling well: Jolley WAS the best of the trio of three-quarters, tackling and running splendidly. Barnes, owing to a knock, did not exhibit his true form, but played a fairly good game. Coming to the Hornets' scrimmagers, Wild and Mellidew were always prominent. The half backs were a little out- classed, although Nolan played exceedingly well. Hastings tried in vain to get away from Jolley, and Buckley was of Immense service to his aide, saving the lines, time after time, when in.danger..

div.head: RUNCORN T. BIRKENHEAD PARK.
div.p: RUNCORN T. BIRKENHEAD PARK.

The match on Saturday between Runcorn and Birkenhead Park was one of no ordinary interest. The clubs were fizhting for the championship of Cheshire, and the Upper Park, where the game was played, was crowded with more than four thousand spectators. Eight hundred persons tra- velled froth Runcorn to Fupport their favourites, and the enthusiastic shouts which broke forth from all sides afford- ed an indication of the excited feelings which animated the spectators. Last year the clubs only met on one occasion, when the "Park" team were victorious. This :year the teams have met twice. The first occasion was at Runcorn, when the borne t,am won a hard game by 'one goal, two tries, and four minors to one minor point. The. second occasion was on Saturday last, when the Runcorn team met their old opponents at Birkenhead. The ball had not been in motion three minutes when Black , for the home team obtained a try. The cheers were deafen- ing as the noted three-quarter planted the tall and the " Parkites" were confident after such a beginning of an easy victory. Cheer after cheer went up as the " Park " team pressed their opponents, but the voices were silent when the visitors by superior pace and stamina get the upper. band. Relieving their lines' the Runcorn forwards dashed towards the opposite goal, where they met with a stubborn resistance. They were not to be refused, and forced a fast game, during which. Andrews got over the line. The "Park" team after this never had a chance. Compelled to play on the defensive for the rest of the game they were overmatched by the rapid tacks of their opponents, who scored one goal, four tries, and four minors, to one try. The result was cheered by the spectators, and the Runcorn contingent left the Park singing the song of the " Jingo party. Between seven and eight honored persons left Runcorn at one o'clock by special train. The team travelled by the same train, and unfortnnatety for them, through the break- down of the engine, they did not arrive on the ground for an hour after the fixed times. The engine failed between Halebank and Speke, whore the line was blocked for nearly an hour, and it was necessary to telegraph to Widnes for an engine to take the train on. Returning by the train at eleven o'clock the supporters of the Runcorn club were in a fever of excitement. On leaving the train they broke song and marched through the streets singing "We've beat the Park before boys, and so we can again." Owing to the accident mentioned above only two thirties were played, and T. Wood kicked off for Birkenhead at four o'clock. Teams —Birkenhead:: C. Holden, back; J. A. Black, E. 0. W. Davies, and D. H. Tweedie, three-quarter backs; L. Holden and F. Spence, half-backs; 1). A. Bingham, A. Dempter, T. Wood, J. Cowen, W. H. Atkinson, P A. Williamson, W. M. Babington, W. S. Callender, and D. Harrison, forwards. Runcorn : T. Woods, back; H. Cawley, H. Speakman, and T. Davies, three-quarter backs ; H. Hughes and H. G. Andrews, half-bad.; W. Wright, W. H. Broady, W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, J. Lewis, G. Wainwright, .1. Clarke, Ja. Barns, and J. Gatley, for- wards.

NOTES BY THE WAY. We were glad to see that fair Turner played for his county last week, and more glad when he was pretty suc- cessful,. notwithstanding what some of the papers sty about his play, others confess that be is a valuable acquisi- tion to the team, being strong, fast, and a good tackler. Our readers will be glad to hear that the slight difference be- tween Turner and the Warrington captain are now smoothed over, a satisfactory explanation having been arrived at. Another thing which speaks well as to how the gentle- men who form the Warrington Committee look to the inter- ests of the players, is that all the first team last week were supplied with a pair of goad boots. First cape, then jerseys, now boots; why not finish the Aig out when you are at it?

The game against Rochdale was a very determined one, screw-scrimmaging being a distinguishing feature, as also was de good back play of the Warrington tea 31. Gilbert got both tries in a very creditable manner.

: The game at Widnes to-day will be a tight one, the pre. ponderence of opinion seems to be that Warrington will about beat the Chemicals. f 1 The West Lancashire v. Westmoreland match will shortly be played. Let the committee take our word for a few good

div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT WHISTON. - A public meeting of Liberals of the Widnes Divil sion was held on Saturday evening in the United Methodist Free Churcb, Whiston, Mr. C. B. Aldrich, of Huyton, occupied the chair, and was supported by Messrs. C. M. Percy, T. Snape, J. Doughan, E. S. Eccles, T. T. Rogers, E. Hughes, J. Storey, H. 13. Shores, &a.

The Chairman said the Liberals invited discussion and co-operation, and wished the working classes to study well the great questions our grand old leader and Grand Old Man—(elontanse)—had placed before the country. He was inclined to think if that question had been better studied at the last election, instead of having a young inexperienced stripling to represent that division they should have had the able services of our friend Mr. Birrell—(cheers)—aad an active Liberal Government instead of a Tory-do-nothing one. (A Voice: "Crowbar.") However, they had done one thing he would remind them of. The pretended friends of Fair Trade had taken mails from Liverpool and given them to a company subsidised by a foreign country. The Liberals of Liverpool—(a Voice: Neville)—had, however, resented that by sending Mr. Ooechen back to London without a seat in Parliament.—(cheers)—and the great Conservative Government would have to subsidiee some other member of Parliament to give him a seat. (Laughter.) Mr. Thomas Snaps moved the first resolution, expressing the conviction that under the guidance of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone a satisfactory measure of self-government for Ireland would be passed into law. The Liberal party would derive encouragement from the resignation of Lord Randolph Churchill, though at the same time they would exercise a more strict vigilance over the policy of the corm- try than before. They could only look for a continuance. and probably an augumentation, of the increase of £8,000,000, which had been made since 1884, and which had changed the £25,900,000 that were then suffi- cient for the army and, navy to the £31,000,000 for which these spending departments clamoured now. The resolution he had to move expressed confidence that under the guidance of Mr. Gladstone a satisfactory settle- ment of the Irish difficulty *mild be effected ere long. Until they had a united Liberal patty this would be no easy task bat he (Mr. Bnape) had great hopes that the outcome of the Round Table Conference would be the reunion of the dissentient Liberals with the bulk of the party. When that was accomplished, a satisfactory measure of,self-government for Ireland would be passed into law, and they would be able to make the ardently-desired progress with those im- portant and much-needed reforms for which the people on this 'ids the bleb Channel were justly becoming impatient. (Applause.) Mr. Eccles seconded the resolution. Speaking of the Plan of Campaign, he expressed an adverse opinion, lie next adverted to the Liberal party, and expressed a hope that there would be a speedy reunion in order to carry out a measure of justice to Ireland. • Mr. C. M. Percy supported the resolution In a vigorous speech, in which he denounced mining royalties. He ree ferred to the Plan of Campaign, saying it ,was desirable to wait for full evidence before condemning it. If that illus- trious statesman, Mr. Gladstone, could afford to wait for further evidence, they could also afford to do so. He was as much in favour of the reunion of the Liberal party as anyone, but it must be on two conditions. The first was that Mr. Gladstone should be leader of the party, and the second was that his policy with regard to Ireland should be accepted. lie (the speaker) was desirous that the Irish question should be settled, in order to make room for gene- ral legislation from a Radical point of view. The resolution was unanimously carried, the proceedings being of an enthusiastic character.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. 131ackhurst, Gibson Brown, W. Houghton, J. Hough- ton, Isherwood, Jolley, Darbyshire Clarke, Ratcliffe, Humphries, Eckersley, Strange, Kilahall, Jones, Swin- ton, Bonnell, Harrison ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Suttan (assistant clerk). HARD ON THE FOWL.

In the course of a'few remarks on the usual list of require- mente for the Workhouse, it was stated that cabbrge.s that had been planted on land in front of the Board Room bad been destroyed by fowl.—Mr. 13ATCLIFFE moved that it should be requested that the fowl be not allowed to go upon the land referred to.—Mr. BLACKHLTEST seconded this pro- posal.—Mr. JOLLEY thought the Board should lay it down that no fowl be kept atthe Workhouse either in confinement or otherwise. He thought it was a lame fowl should be allowed to destrof the produce of so large an area to please the fad of anybody. Let them forbid fowl to be kept within the area of that Workhouse. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. ISHER- WOOD said that he would agree witb Mr. Jolley if the Schools were included in the resolution. (Hear, hear.)—Mr JOLLEY said he was quite willing that that should be done, because he believed that irregularities would creep in at the Schools also.—lt was then resolved that the keeping of fowl at both the Workhouse and the Schools should be pro- hibited.

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes stated that the doctor bad ad- vised that for the present no children should be gent from the Workhouse to the Schools, as there were a few cases of measles in the house.—Mr. BROWN moved, and Mr. ISHER. WOOD seconded, the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to.

SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that tbe doctor bad reported the health of the children to be very good.—On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Alt% RATCLIFFE, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
It was reported that school fees were allowed in 125 cases, 103 of which were old and 22 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. EnowN, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: TILE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE.
div.p: TILE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE.

A letter addressed to the Chairman, and signed by the organising secretary of the proposed Imperial Institute, was read, and stated that he bad been directed by the Prince of Wales to enclose, for the perusal of the Board, and, it was hoped, favourable consideration, a copy of a letter which had been addressed to the Lord Lieutenants throughout the United Kingdom. He would be pleased to learn that he would be disposed, in pursuance of the suggestion contained in the letter, to ask members of the Board who represented parishes in the rural districts, not comprised in the limits of a municipal borough or urban district, to act as local committees for his or their own parish, and to act himself as chairman of the whole number, and as their representative on the council or general committee, which it was trusted would be formed by the Lord Lieutenant. —The CRAIRMAN said he did not know how to deal with that matter. Perhaps it the members were to think it over they would be ready te express an opinion at the next meeting—Mr. HARRISON: I should suggest that the least said the soonest mended. (Laughter.)—Mr. JOLLEY thought the feeling in general was that what was to be done in connection with the jubilee should be done locally. (Hear, hear.) There were hun- dreds of thousands in the country who would never see the Imperial Institute. He moved that the letter be con- sidered that day six mentlas.—The CLERK: You should not pot it in that form,—The CHAIRMAN again suggested that the letter be left over for a fortnight; it might be lost in that time. (Laughter.)—The suggestion of the Chairman was agreed to. THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S CASE.

The CHAIRMAN said there was a letter from the Local Government Board bearing upon the question that was be- fore the Board at its previous meeting, when Mr. Henley (the LOCAI Ghvernment Board inspector) was present. Mr. Henley had a communication to make, and he requested that it might be heard in camera, that was that the reporters might not be present. The communication he (the chair- man) had was a continuation of the matter formerly dealt with, and he would, therefore, ask the Board whether or not the reporters should be asked to take no notice of it.—Mr. BLACKHORST thought it would be better to leave the matter to the discretion of the reporters. He thought it would have been much better both for the credit of the Board and for the information of the public if the whole of the materials were made public through the press. He moved that the reporters be left to use their own discretion.—Mr: Jogs HouGalore seconded the proposal.—Mr. JOLLEY said. that seeing they eat with closed doors on the previous oc- casion, he thought nothing but mischief could come from a a half report. He, therefore, moved that the reporters be asked to take no notes of what might be disclosed that morn- ing in connection with the Workhouse Master's affairs.— Mr. IlannisoN said that in his own mind he was in favour of the reporters remaining in the room on the previous oc- casion and using their own discretion—and as a rule their discretion generally turned•out to be right—but seeing that they at with closed doors at the former meeting, he was in favour of Mr. Jolley's motion.—lt was then agreed that the reporters should be requested not to take notes of the pro- ceedings. The correspondence from the Local Government Board referred to by the Chairman consisted of a copy of a letter Sent by that Authority to Mr. Mackie, the Workhouse mabter, in which he was again asked to place his resigna- tion in the heeds of the Guardians; and also of a copy of a memorial in favour of Mr. Mackie which has recently been largely signed and sent to the Local Government Board. Considerable objection was made to the statements con- tained in the preamble cf the memorial, and the Clerk was directed by the Board to write to the Local Government Board pointing out what appeared to them to be incorrect. A resolution was also passed asking the Local Government Board to bring the matter to an end one way or another as early as possible. THE DEATH OF MR. BROADBENT. ' CHAIRMAN said they had all '

The ay had all been grieved and shocked to hear of the death of Mr. C. Broadbent, who, al- though at the time of his death was not an elected member of that Board, yet had been in the habit of attending as an ex.o.ilicio member. He mentioned that the funeral would take place on the following day should any gentleman wish to attend. A vote of condolence with the widow and family would, no doubt, be proposed at the meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority, of which Mr. Broadbent was chairman. The relief cases were then proceeded with.
