div.p: xttuts to tut editor.
THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT,

Sir, —lt seems to me that we shall have to be careful, or else we shall end by placing Warrington in a somewhat ridiculous position. First, we have a statue of her Majesty promise& and then because of the sad death of the sculptor selected, this promise is withdrawn, as if there were no other sculptor, making it appear that it was not exactly loyalty to her Majesty, so much as a desire to place a lump of money in one particular individual's pocket. Well, let us be thank- ful we are spared the infliction of an heroic figure; we shall get over it. During the past couple of years an agitation has been carried on, having for its object the making of Warrington Library lute a Free Lending Library. What has been a healthy feature of the movement, may perhaps account for the little support it has received from the "classes." The movement, from beginning to end, so far, has bad the hearty approval of the "masses." It can be no secret to anycne who cares to read and to study the signs of the times, that there has been a great awakening amongat the people daring the long number of years during which we have had what is called a "Depression in trade." The toilers and mailers are becoming alive to the fact that there is a great deal going on in the world of which they themselves are made to bear the burden, that the more faci- lities there are for reading, and the more a taste for reading is cultivated, the more power the people will get into their hands, but with all the knowledge the people may get, they feel they want understanding. Hitherto a brutal power, got only out of the labour of the people, has been sufficient for keepina society in something like an orderly state. It Is time this was ended. We see around us evidences that not only political parties, but the relationship hitherto exis- ting between labour and capital, are undergoing a change. We are wearying of the forces that are constantly driving men to do those things they ought not to, do, and to leave undone those things they ought to do. There is no class at this time justified in pluming itself On its superior knowledge. Specialists we have by the thous- and, but the power of to-day proceeds only from the possession of the profits of toil. What we want is the death and burial of ignorance, and in its place we want an intel- ligent guiding power. We can only have this by encoura- ging the people to read and think, and making them under- stand that they have a stake in the nation's welfare. Read- ing is not to be looked upon as a luxury; it is a duty which every man ought to attend to, as a duty to his fellowman, and ass feature in his life's work to enable him to leave the world better than he found it. There are people who look upon the demana for a Free Library as something so Out- rageous that they hesitate not to give it the stigma of So- cialism, forgetting that Socialism is fast becoming an ack- nowledged feature in the economical government of the world. We see each winter, when frost sets in, and bard times come upon us, soup kitchens formed. Why is this done? Because we cook and provide food on a large scale much cheaper than on a small scale. The townspeople buy the gas works because they know the purchase will benefit the many, and if rightly managed will supply cheaper gas; same with the water works; and so we go on all round until we reach the, Baths and Library question: It is mere madness to keep twenty thousand books in the hands of a fraction of the inhabitants, when the minds of thousands are starving for want of coming in contact with the true and beautiful ideas now mouldering on the book shelves. It seems to be characteristic of the Englishman to wait 'until disaster overtakes him before be makes an effort to save himself. There is one thing he is willing to do, that is, appoint Royal Commission. Then he thinks he has dune his duty, and takes no further notice. Working-men, and their employers, would be surprised to know what is going , on in other countries with regard to facilities fer study. I I say employers, because I take it for granted they do not know, or else they would onl 7 be too glad to encourage the I aspirations of their working-men in the desire for study. In France, Germany, and Italy, every manufacturing town, I and almost every' large industrial establishment, has a large library free to all Looking through the Report of the Royal I Commission on Technical Instruction, I note that it is al- Most impossible to find a town without its Free Library, and this, too, not of a trashy character. For instance, take the Dresden Industrial Art School, which receives an annual I grant of £2000; a library of art works for which the annual grant is £750 This school has an annual grant, for books and art of £5750. Mr. Isaac Holden. a well-knows name in Bradford, owner of large wool combing establishments in France, has con- nected with his places at Croix and Rheims "English read- ing rooms and free libraries well stocked with books." In Italy every manufacturing centre is well provided with libraries. At Beilla, a town of 15,000 inhabitants, there is a library of 10,000 volumes the gift of the leading manu- facturers of the place. England only holds her place now as a manufacturing country in consequence of the physical strength of her sons. In the higher walks of mental and art training she is losing ground, and it is through tbe grasp- ing selfishness of her manufacturers, who care for nothing but making their" pile," and then retiring to enjoy a " well earned repose." A deal of stress is laid on the fart that we in Warrington have an art museum, by those who do not encourage thet free lending library scheme. We have, but what of that? Surely we are not to nurse it until it becomes a white elephant. Money is spent on what is called art, that might as well be thrown away. I recently saw two "Turner's" that would not have found hanging room in a barn. No one could make out what the pictures were, yet we had to pay insurance and carriage for the daubs. With all this, I strongly support the Art Gallery, and hope to see it well supported, but not at the expense of a Free Library. Liter- ature first, and art mast follow. I have spoken strongly, Mr. Editor. for I see this question or a Free Lending Library will have to be fought out, and we might as well commence speaking straight at once. We acknowledge there are financial difficulties in the way, but it the difficulties are met squarely and fairly they may le brushed out of the way. That, at any rate, is the opinion of CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: "WAIT A LITTLE LONGER."
div.p: "WAIT A LITTLE LONGER."

Sir,-1 gatherit:e-m-.MT-H-a-n-dilsi;it;Tthat he is not at all disposed to deprive me of the little consolation I receive from blowing the steam off in the columns of a newspaper. This is well, because the more•opportunities we louts have for easing our minds, the more likely are we to "rest and be thankfol " in the position to labial it has pleased God to call ca. I should have been better pleased with Mr. Gandy's letter if he bad left out altogether Mr. Mackenzie's book. It rests just at my shoulder as I write. Written six years ago, it has become ancient history. What we have to con- sider is--how does the machinery affect the people to-Jay? What my friend John says respecting the collier of to-day •and the collier of half a century ago is quite outside the argument. Were it necessaryi could harrow up the souls of your readers by quoting largely from the reports given, and speeches made to both Houses of Parliament in 1842 respecting the condition of the women and children em.' ployed l mines. The materials lie ready to hand for this, but what then? Suppose we take the advice of the Individualist patty, and withdraw Government supervision and inspectorship of coal mines, how long should we be before the avarice of employers and the demands of capital would open the pita again to women and children, and again should we have sexless creatures paving their tribute at the shrine of improved machinery. Mr. Gandy gave your readers the extract from my letter respecting the fifty" handa" giving way to machinery. He made no special remark anent the matter, but rushed off into generalisations. It was as well he did so l be could have given no satisfactory answer, for the fact remains, 50 " hands " are discharged to make room for machinery. And not... ppose we COOl9 to the great question as to the amount of happiness that machinery spreads amongst •

us. It is of no use to make comparisons between to-day and yesterday as to whether my great grandmother was ' better or worse off in the world than what I era to-day. What I know as an absolute fact is, that taking progress in its most universal aeon.', we to-day have wants and aspira- tions that were unknown to our ancestors. If Mr. Gandy and your readers will study Professor Roger's works on English labour, they will find that the peasantry of England under the Rouses of York and Lancaster, and during the early years of the first of the Tudor Kings, were by no means the miserable half-starved s•rfs genrally supposed. If Mr. Gandy ever studied Elizabethan literature, or accompanied the merry travellers through the "Canterbnry Tales," he would know that in those good old d vs there was a free- spoken, well-fed population. Or, if these suit not his palate, take Cobbett and Kingsley, and,fhen perhaps the good old days will receives little more mercy at his hands. Merely studying the history of labour during the nineteenth cen- tury is misleading. The artisan, the middle-man, and the employer, as we know him, is the product of the age of improved machinery, which in its earlier days carries a thousand long and ghastly tales. When machinery was in its infancy, and the inventive faculty in man was all bat dormant, struggles were of a fiercely wild character, and it never entered the mind of man to lay restrictions, either of a moral or legislative character, on the methods te be pursued in production. But with the development of steam power grew the selfiah and base Nations in man, and the greed for riches drove out of the manufacturer's breast all love for his kind; in fact, to such a degree, that men like John Bright in their love for Free Trade lost all human in- stincts.

I, no more than Mr. Gandy, am prepared to condemn In toto the use of machinerr; but this I assert, that we • are now passing through the most important crisis that labour and capital ever saw, and that when we or our chil- dren see the end of it, machinery will be used for the bene- fit of the people, and not to create riches for the few; and that it will be used for the manufacture' of things needed, and not for the manufacture of things merely for sale. I know quite as well as Mr. Gandy bow much better off we 'are through the 111141 Of 'new and improved machinery." I know that our grocers' shop could not be filled with good and cheap fruit from the east, and cheap hams and bacon from the west, without it. I also know that the same steam ship that brings these good things over carries also a troop ef black, miserable wretches, down in the hot and stifling stoke hole; that her shafting and machinery, followed up, would show us the miserable under-paid puddler; that her fires are kept going by sending men down into the bowels of the earth, and rewarding them with ties magnificient sum of las a week! I most confess that Mr. Gandy's letter knocked all the poetry out of me; it seemed so full of a self satisfaction that appeared to say--"Pve done well; Why does'nt every body else do well ?" Machinery is a wend-erful power; it might be the servant of man, but it is fast becoming his , master. Our grandmothers used to be content with their stitching and knitting, and to make a dress was no difficult task. We invented the sewing machine ; now it requires an artist to cut it out, and • machinist to pot it together, and when the complicated thing is made and hoisted into its I place, there to rest on its mechanical contrivance, we are called upon to pay, in more senses than one our tribute to the inventive faculty of man. The dress one, that used to be made on the quite country side, is now made in a fac- tory. Machinery, attracts around it, like the candle the moth, all its victims. Walk through the narrow streets sur- rounding Cockhedire factory, or any other factory, for they are all alike, and please tell me, Mr. Gandy, how you would like to be told that von, were you residing there, were I happier and better off than your forefathers? If the bene- fits derived are not satisfactory, get a job in a weaving shed and work ten or a dozen hours in an atmosphere composed of steam and dust, so that when you leave work at night, the very hair on your head is like a mop, and your throat longs for a gill to clear the road. Oh, yes, the blessings of machinery are innumerable! Go into a rolling mill and ask what is the difference in the turn out, between to-day and twenty-five years ago; then it might be seven tons a turn, now it is nearer forty. Don't ask about the wages, because that would complicate the matter. You might go to the workmen's homes and ask the wires, and if you want to make things lively, suggest to the wife how much better off she is now than she use to was. If not satisfied vet, ex- tend your travels and go into a wire mill, and if you are fortunate enough to catch any of the men at work, repeat the queetion, and you will find that improved machinery keeps the men at home three days out of every six. Per- haps, Mr. Editor, this is the secret of the Free Library agitation; the men have so much time on their bands, and so little money in their pockets, that they want to read to kill time; no wonder. Now,then,we have had the pit, the mill, and the factory ; we only want the farm labourer, and sure enough, air, he Is to the front, We plough with a steam plough, reap with a steam reaper, and gather in the harvest with steam and horse machines. We thrash it, too, with a steam thrashing machine. Sir, there is no poetry in all this. I could rush off into poetic freuzy, but what room is there for pastorals? We shall never again hear the "thresher's weary flingin'- tree."

I see Mr. Morrie is going to try to give us some infirma- Con on the question of machinery. I beg be will let us have something original, and for the present, perhaps, Mr. Gandy and I may bottle up, only eaying for myself that I acknowledge that there are rare benefits and pleasure only to be had through the use of machinery. The surgeon is enabled to give relief to the sufferers through the use ot instruments made by delicate machines; the microscopist would be without his instrument were it not for another and more complicated machine, and I suppose Mr. Stanley would be without the Maxim gun,' The M4XIIII gun, See, how the savages scatter and run. Before very long there will scarce be one. Where the '„Christian hero,' the friend of Peace, Takes deadly arm At his human game. Puts up his prayer and levels his piece!" Mr. Gandy may see from this tit .t the blessings resulting from machinery are out-balanced by the curses, or at least, I think, he would had I a little more rc am to talk about the splendid war ships this most Christian nation is pos. sessed of.

_ The fact is, sir, as I have said before, we are going through a vials in which machinery is a very important factor; labour-saving machinery is causiag a plethora of labour; hence "the unemployed." Capitalists, by compet- ing with each other, have largely reduced the price of com- modities, and have themselves reduced their profits, wages have risen, not in actual money, but In value. Interest on money will die out, profits will cease; we shall make what we want, and hurrah for the millennium
COLIN CLOUT.

Hicks, Hargreaves, and Company, of Bol- ton.
THE LOSS OF THE KAPUNDA.

The Central News says Messrs. Tunder Anderson and Co. have received Important telegrams from Brazil, whiok Set at rest all question as to the identity of the persons saved from the ill-fated emigrant ship Kapunda. The list, as finally revised and confirmed, shows that eight of the crew and eight passengers have been saved. All hopes of there being other survivors must now, it is feared, be aban- doned. Inquiries have been made at every likely port along the South American coast without eliciting information. It is of course just possible that some survivors may be on board vessels homeward bound, but the hope is a very slen- der one.

TO TIIE MEMORY OF JOHN CONNISON. We grieve to think that he kas passed, In manhood's prime away, That we no more shall view his eye, Bright as a sunny day. The genial and honest heart, That we have loved so well, Revealed itself in friendly smile, That could no falsehood tell. No low ambition stirred his soul With enmity and strife; Contentedly in peace he lived A useful happy life. Too large his soul for selfish aims, That make life's troubles strong; Too kind his sympathetic heart • To do another wrong. Beyond the bounds of time and sense, His soul has passed away, Snatched from this erring, chequered world , To God's eternal day.
S. KENYON.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM MR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The official rate was on Thursday reduced by the direc- tors of the Bank of England from sto 4 per cent. This step indicates that at any rate pressure for money either from America or the continent is not anticipated for the present. This step, however, has had no material effect on the Stock Exchange, where panic has followed panic ever since the .7ar rumours first caused the Exchanges of Europe to tremble. At the present time it is worse than useless to particularise any individual stuck as being under their in- trinsic value. The fall in prices has affected every class of security, and the irony of the situation is, that apart from those stocks more directly concerned with the nations that are assumed as likely to be affected by war, some of the stocks that are likely to derive actual benefit by war have suffered most. Home rails, especially the Southern passen- ger lines, have fallen day after day. Ai a matter of record, the traffic returns show an average increase, and the im- proved dividends of the last half-year ought rather to have sent prices up. Investors would do well, howevb7, not to be scarQd out of their stocks at the present time, as prices could not go worse were war actually declar.d and viewed calmly, the probabilities are, on the whole, in favour of peace. It is not pleasant to see one's investments made the shuttlecock of gamblers, at the same time the public have only to "sit tight" and the gamblers will be the sufferers, and any sympathy on their account is enrireT wasted

„ Tbe long deferred issue of Messrs. Allsopp ands Sons has at last been made with a capital of £3,300,000, divided equally into debenture, preference and ordinary shares. All sorts of reports hive been in circulation as to when this core- pany would see daylight, and as late as Tuesday it was positively announced that it has been shelved till April. However, on Wednesday it was officially stited that the company would be 'Out” on Thursday, and the shires were actually dealt in on Wednesday at 53 premium. I What chance the public generally have of obtaining an al- lotment remains to be seen, but their chances are remote in- deed, as the capital has already been subscribed over and over again. One of the most extraordinary sizhts ever witnessed was outside the company's offices on Ihursday. It had been stated that prospectuses could be had at nine o'c'ock, and by eight people Logan congregating, and being situated in a narrow court the approach to the office was difficult. A detachment of fifty policemen were required to keep anything like order, and soon after eleven it was an- nounced that no more prospectuses were to be had. How- ever, a further issue was made in the afternoon, and the newsvendors were selling them in the adjoining streets at as ' high a pricn a.' 23 6d each and getting it readily. There is a craze just now for brewery investment., but it is to be hoped we shall not have a repitetion of the Guiness allot- ment.

A company has been fo,nned for the purpose of trading in Australian wines. Investors should ascertain fully the pro• babilities of the sales of this class of wine before investine, as they would otherwise ba disappointed if the sales were not as they were led to anticipate.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. Miscsu.semous.—The Standing Orders Committee was appointed.--A bill to amend the Appellate Jariadiction Act was read a firat time, and the Pluralities Act Amend- ment Bill was read a second time.—Christchurch Charter Bill was _read a thiri time.
The House adjourned ; half-Daat four. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'clock

QUESTIONS, &h.—Mr.-PI-C.-TON gave notice on an early day to call attention to railway passengers' duty, with a view to its revision.—Barcn DE WORMS, replying to Mr. Vincent Howard, said the unfortunate ship Kapunda had fully complied with the law as regarded life-saving appara- tus, and the authorities had no power to demand more.— Mr. E. STkNHOPE, replying to Colonel Lawrie, said the Volunteer Committee recommended an increase of the capi- tation grant of two shillings for three marching days. THE FIGHTING IT XlSSOweil —Sir J. FERGUSON, re- plying to Mr. Legh, said they had no other intelligence of affairs at Massowah than that stated by Count Kobilant in , the Italian Chamber, viz., that according to a despatch re- ceived from the commandant at Massowab, January 2fith, a serious conflict had taken place with the Abyssinians, who were driven back after four hours combat, and that, next , day, a column was sent to revictual Saati, and was attacked by the Abyssinians and destroyed. THE ADDRESS—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. CREMER, who moved an amendment deprecating the continue occupation of Egypt by British troops, and recommendinv her Majesty to take immediate steps for recalling the whole of her forces. He insisted that the British working classes were being highly taxed in order to secure payments to great financiers and holders of Egyptian bonds -Sir W. LAwsoN supported the amendment. lie said their whole work in Egypt had been one long night- mare of blundering and bloodsbed.—Sir J. FERGUSON said the British were in Egypt for the benefit of the Egyptian p.ople. The British force was shortly to be reduced to five thousand, and the native army would also be reduced from seventeen to ten th‘usand men.—The debate was cantinued by Mr. Caine. Col. Duncan, Dr. Clark. Sir R.Temple, Mr. C. Dalrymple, and other members.

RITNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held on Thursday under the presidency of Mr. P. Speakman. Present—Messrs. Taylor, Lake, Lightburn, Grine, Hankinsen, Dobson, Shaw, Imison, E, Marshall. (secretary), F. McDougall (medical officer), M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: FIELLTH OF' THE TOWN.
div.p: FIELLTH OF' THE TOWN.

The number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amount to 24. Of these two were inquest cases, and of r:t. remainder 7 were due to bronchitis, 4 to natural decay, 2 ta convulsions, consumpti m, disease of abdominal origin, and otte eaeh to premature birth, disease of the heart, disease of the liver, inflammation of the lungs, and one to collapse. The above deaths showed an average deatlarate of a little over 16 per 1.000, and excluding the inquests, of a fraction over 15 per 1,000. The lowest age registered was 20 days, and the oldest 06 years. There was not a death from Infectious disease registered during the, past month, and he had reason to believe that the town was free from the Zymotic class of diseases.—The report was considered very satisfactory.

div.head: – FINANCE.
div.p: - FINANCE.

The minutes of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr; Dobson, stated that the receipts for the month amounted to £421 la 2J, and accounts amounting to £BO5 is 7d were passed for payment. It was recommended that the private improvement talances, amounting to £27 5s ld, be written off as irrecoverable. ',HEALTH COMMITTEE,-THE HOSPITAL. -

This committee recommended that the sanction of the Local GoVernment Board be obtained under Section 133 of the Public Health Act, 1875, to the payment of the sum of £l2 103 to Dr. MacLennote, for professional attendance on hSaunders, of Bridge-street. It was also the familyro recommended of B. that the stun of 33 per week be paid to Mrs Bowles as retaining fee as nurse at the hospital, instead of Is per week as at present —ln moving the adoption of the minutes Mr. Lighburn said the case of Saunders was quite exceptional. The whole of his family had been attacked by typhoid fever, and to prevent the spread of the die-ase, his shop had been closed, and the clothes of the family had been destroyed. The man's means of living was therefore cat off, and he was ruined financially. The Government Inspector had expressed himself well pleased with the manner in which the cases had been isolated, and the mode in which the town had been disinfected.—Mr. Taylor secon- ded the motion.—Mr. Shaw said the Board had spent a con- siderable sum of money in erecting a hospital for the put- poss'of isolating, cases of this description, and it ought to be one of the primary considerations of the committee to remove patients to the place provided for them, and not attempt to make every shop or dwelling-house into a hos- pital. Mr_ Lightburn replied that the doctor when the consent of the family was obtained said removal would cause their death.—Mr. &rice asked if the Board had power to compel removal to the hospital.—The Law Clerk replied that if there was not sufficient accommodation they could ask the Parties for an otder of removal.—Mr. Lake said the hospital should if poseible be used for all cases of this kind. There was no (;oubt a strange antipathy to hospitals. It was a pity this should be so, and it was for the Board or the Com- missioners to show the public that it would be better for the patients to be removed and attended at the hospital. He was afraid the med.cal men thought the hospital inconve- niently situated,and proposed to attend the patients in their own heme. Unless the Board could get the medical men to follow the action of the Commissioners in this matter there was no chance for the hospital.—After some further discussion the minutes we!nad.Emted.

THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. Alluding to the subject of the Queen's Jubilee, the Chair- man said he had no definite plan to bring before the mem- bers. Ho was present in London at the Conference with re- gard to the Imperial Institute and saw the Prince of Wales. lie did not think His Highness raw him. (Laughter)— Mr. Taylor : No fault of yours, Mr. Chairman. (Renewed laughter.)—The Chairman said he happened to arrive late, and so missed the Royal bow. The Prince of Wales' great thought was for the Imperial Institute. He (the Chair- man) thought, as good and Royal subjects, they in Run- corn ought to do something to commemorate the Jubilee of their beloved Queen. Public baths had been mentioned I from time to time by candidates for the suffrages of the ratepayers, but up to now nothing had been done.—Mr. Lightburn : I beg von pardon. The Health Committee have had plans presented to them, and we have it in hand. —The Chairman said he was glad to hear that "Jubilee baths" would be provided—whether they were by the rate- payers or by the gift of some gentleman—of course, they were not very particular so. long as they got baths. He heartily hoped the Board would co-operate with him in do- ing something to commemorate the JabiLe of her Majesty. He proposed to call a public meeting. but he did not think it wise to do so until there was' some definite proposition to bring forward. Mr. Lake remarked that there were two objects the town bad been striving for for a great many years, which he thought would be beneficial modes of celebrating the jubilee. One of these was an accident hospital and a dispensary, and he believed such an institution was extremely useful, and highly appreciated in every district where one was estab- lished. He thought he knew a source from which a small income might be derived for its support, and subscriptions for this object would be given se freely as for anything by

A HELM RAILWAY Itscnnurr.—On Monday, at Eddie- 1 bury Petty Sessions, Alexander Malcomson, q tramp, was charged with riding without a ticket, on the London and I North-Western Hallway on the 28th January.—Prisoner I pleaded guilty. Asked why he took the ticket from Liver- pool to Edge Hill, he said he did it to passs the barrier at Liverpool.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was fined LI, I Or 14 days' imprisonment. —LIBERAL MErrinr4.—The Libera's of Kingsley had a very successful meeting in the National Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. James Tomkinson, of Willington j Hall, gave a very instructive address on the Irish question, ,1 I dealing with the bugbears of separation, religions intoler- ance, cost of land purchase, the Irish labour question, ckc., j in a very effective manner. Mrs. Tomkinson, in a few re- marks on the same question, made a great impression oh the audience, after which she gave an interesting address on the., "Good old times." Mr. Clegg. of Runcorn, was most hu- morous in his remarks on mistakes of the Government.— Mr. Ankers and Mr. B. Rniveton supported the previous speakers.—The meeting was then brought to a close with a vote of thanks to the chairman. Warner. The total number present was be- tween sixty and seventy. Tasteful decorations, together j with a variety of curiosities, and objects of interest to per- sons of musical taste, gave the hall an agreeable aspect. the manufacturers and the working classes. It seemed to show a lack of humanity to send an injured man to Liver- pool or Chester; or that be should be at the mercy of a medical man who wished to collect his fee before he would tie up a broken leg. The other object mentioned by Mr. Lake was the carrying out of the alterations to Waterloo. road. The work wanted doing badly, was quite feasible, and would be eminently beneficial.—Mr. Lightburu doped- bed the steps taken some years ago to form an accident I hospital, and he thought it would be an excellent and practical way of commemorating the jubilee, to establish such an institution.—Mr. Hankineon approved of Mr. Lake's suggestion as to the accident hospital. Public baths, however, be thought would be the most popular ob- ject with the people. He also thought some festivities should be provided for the children, accompanied with a distribution of medals.—Mr. Grice had no doubt arrange- ments would be made to make the year memor- able to the school children ; and they wanted something more substantial to celebrate the jubilee. Was it intended that baths should be erected by voluntary subscriptions or by the rates.—Mr. Lightburn said his idea was to raise as much as possible by voluntary subscriptione, and the balance between the cost of the baths and the amount raised to come out of the rates. Mr. Lightburn mentioned the great success that bad attended the baths at Nantwich, through the use t,f brine there, and brine being conveni- ently available at Runcorn he was of opinion that baths in the latter town would be equally successful.—Mr. Shaw considered the suggestion of Mr. Lake with regard to Waterloo Bridge a good one. There were plans and every- thing ready for the work being carried out, and the only thing wanted was the sanction of the Board. The formation of an accident hospital would be an important step. He did not think they would provide for anything outside their own small area. There was a grand opportunity fcr the chairman to distinguish himself, and he hoped he was go- ing to do so. (Laughter.)-1 he Chairmon : I have no doubt I shall. (Laughter.)—Mr. Shaw, referring to baths, said he did not object to them, but in small places like Runcorn they were a great expense upon the rates. It was Important that they should not put upon the rates a per- manent charge which would not be appreciated.—Mr. Lightburn did net think that would mean such a great charge, and there would boa saving in the cleanliness and health of the inhabitants.—Mr. Meadowcroft said he was glad to hear that the chairman intended to dis• tinguish himself this jubilee year. He could not folloW a better example than that set by Sir A. B. Walker, but in a more moderate sense ; and he was sure it would add to his (the chairman's) fame, as well as his respected name in Runcorn if be were to make up his mind to complete the cathedral at Newtown. (" Oh," and laughter.) That was a structure that would be of con- siderable benefit when completed, and would always be a monument to his munificience. Alluding to the questions thrown eut that morning, Mr. Meadowcreft suggested that they should be left for further consideration. Mr. Dobson said the party that Mr. Meadowcroft belonged to ought to do their own work and let the public have the benefit of the church.—Mr. Lake : We shall have It opened in the course of a few mon,hs, Mr. Dobson—Ultimately a committee consisting ot the Chairmao, Messrs. Lake, Light- barn, Meadowcroft, Shaw, and Dobson was appointed to con- sider the subject end report.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The first meeting of the new Board was held yesterday. Pre ent—Dr. McDougall, Messrs W. Handley, F. A. Lake, E. Imison, S. C. Beckett, James Pritchard, and F. Rigby (clerk).
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The first meeting of the new Board was held yesterday. Pre ent—Dr. McDougall, Messrs W. Handley, F. A. Lake, E. Imison, S. C. Beckett, James Pritchard, and F. Rigby (clerk).
APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.

On the proposition of Mr. W. Handley, seconded by Mr. Lake, Mr. James Pritchard was unanimously appointed chairman for the ensuing three years. Upon taking the chair Mr. Pritchard said it would be his endeavour to con- duct the business of the Board so as to merit a continuance of their confidence. He trusted the members would work together to advance the educational interests of the commu- nity.—Yather Fennelly was unanimously appointed to the position of vice-chairman. on the motion of M.r. Imison, se- conded by Mr. Handley.
TIME OF MEETING. If was recommended that the meetings of the Board should be held in future at 7 p.m. on the first Tuesday in each month.

A LOSS ON THE SCHOOLS. Mr. Beckett drew attention to the fact that the balance sheet showed that the Board had lost £313 on their schools during the past year. As the other schools in the town paid their way this was a remarkahle thing. The Chairman explained that that loss was more apparent than real, of the amount named at least £2OO ought to have coma under capital charges, including the purchase of furniture, gas fittings, and alterations to Mill Brow School. Then 'the Government Inspector refused to give a twelvemonths' grant for those children who had been educated at Mill Brow School for six months, and then transferred to Green. v wa-road School. Again, the schools were new, and as the other schools in the town were filled, they had to take in the neglected children who could not earn grant. They could not expect a school to pay the first year. But the teachers had been informed that better results would be ex- peeled for the present year.—Dr. McDougall said the Board should have taken such action that the loss of six months' grant would have been avoided.—The Clerk said the Board could not help thems9lves.

RESIGNLTION OP THIR The Clerk said it was twelve years that day since he undertook the office of clerk, and with a great deal of plea- sure to himself and to those with whom he had acted, be had continued in the position the whole of that period. He now wished to thank Mr. Pritchard, who was the one remaining of the original members, for his kindness, and to express his intention of resigning his position in three months from that da} The Board then considered the attendance returns.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANIIARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANIIARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Patton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present : Colonel Ashton (chairman), the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Major Fox, Messrs. E. Aaron, Lewis, Mclntyre, Smith, Whitlow. Knowles, Parr, Hadfield, Campkio, H. Percival, Brondrett, H. Lina- ker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk),. and J. Harring- ton (inspector). WE3TON POINT SnwEn.—The Nuisance Inspector re- ported that in making an eximination of the sewer laid through the ground and works belonging to the Mersey Salt and Brine Company be found that the company in their levelling operations had completely buried the larupholes to the sewer. The manholes were also getting very low, and he greitly feared that in the course of time they too would share the same fate as the lampholes. If such I levelling operations continued the tops of both lampholes I and manholes should be raised accordingly, but upon whom the duty of raising, retaining, and protecting devolves was a question for the consideration of the Authority. There were also two walls, ands building, which appeared to be intended for the use of the workmen.—Mr. Aaron, who had accompanied the inspector, confirmed this statement, and said tbatanother part of the sewer was covered.with 12 to 15 feet of earth, and whenever tbe sewer needed cleaning it would be a serious matter. Weston had been very wrong- fully dealt with in times past, but the township was now getting a little justice, and he hoped this matter would be promptly dealt with.—As the law clerk had drawn up the agreement, the subject was referred for his consideration and report.

div.head: EXCITING FIRES AT RUNCORN
div.p: EXCITING FIRES AT RUNCORN

About eleven o'clock on Friday night several gentlemen were passing along Duke-street, when they observed the shop of William Slut Heroes to be on fire. The flames rapilv spreading, had attacked the roof, and the house was filled with dense volumes of smoke. The family were made aware of their perilous position, and as it was impossible to make use of the stairs, Mrs. Shallcrnss dropped her youngest child through the upper window, and it was caught by those below. Mrs. shallcroes then made her exit in a similar manner. She then made it known that two children occupied the back bedroom, and at once Mr J. B. Holland, sub-manager at Parr's Bank, gallantly pro- ceeded to their rescue, but discovered that they had been saved by their father. Means were then taken to subdue the flames, and after an hout'S hard work the fire was com- pletely extinguished without the assistance of the fire brigade. The property was insured. The Theatre is in very close proximity to the shop, and had not the fire been se opportunely discovered, that building would have been in great danger of destruction. On Tuesday morning the business premiies Of the Barley Mow Hotel, Church-street, were partly destroyed by fire. The landlord, Mr. John B:undell, lsecame aware that the building was on fire about a quarter to three, and the dense volumes of smoke effectually barring the escape of the family by the Staircase, he gave an alarm from the bedroom window. P.C. Corbett ran to give information at the police office, and P.C. Povey remained on the spot to rander what aid he could. By the advice of his wife Mr. Blundell got securely hold of the corner of a blanket, and Mrs Blundell retaining hold of the other end, he lowered himself through the bedroom window, but he nevertheless had a drop of eight feat to the ground. and he severely sprained his ankle. By this time Inspector Millington and Sergeant Cooper hail arrived on the scene. An attempt was made to force cpen the door, but it did not succeed. A glass panel was there- fore smashed, and Constable Miy went through the aper- ture thus formed, and unbolted the door. The flames and smoke were such, however, that the idea of rescuing the family in the upper chambers by that way was abandoned, and as quickly as possible two ladders were obtained from the establishment of Mr. Yarwood in Lock-street, and placed against the windows. They were ascended by Constables May and Povey, who each returned with a child in his arms, and then May reascended and fetched Mrs. Bluodell in safety. The entire family were kindly received into the house ofeMr. Stone, the shoe- maker. During the time of this exciting rescue, the fire had been rapidly gaining ground, and messengers were des- patched in all directions to warn the firemen, whilst the fire bell was rung. Hundreds of persons assembled • in tke street, which was lit up with a lurid glare, but through the admirable exertions of the police, the quietest order was maintained, and the ,bzigade on their arrival at 3-30 wera not hampered in the performance of their duty in the slightest. Deputy bnperintendent Wright, who was soon after joined by his father, Superintendent Wright, directed the labours of their men with good judgment, and a stream of water was quickly pouring on the burning mass. Some difficalty was met with in fixing one of the hydrants to the main, but they were overcome, and two hose pipes were working from Church-street, and one from the rear of the building in Cooper - street was soon at work. An hour later, so great was the pressure of the water, the flames were entirely extinguished,

The large bar was entirely gutted, and all the furniture hi the bar parlour and commercial-room was almost entirely consumed.'. The bedroom over the bar caught fire, but the inroad of the flames was quickilk stopped, and the upper rooms are little if at all damaged. The exterior brickwork is considerably damaged, and so fierce were the flames that the woodwork of the shops opposite are scorched and burnt. The damage is stated at about £750, which is covered by insurance in the Alliance Office. The stock, worth between £6O and £7O, is, unfortunately, not moored. The police present, who rendered good assistance, were Superinmndent Hollingworth, Inspector Millington, Ser- geant CoopP,, and P.C.'s May, Corlett, Millington, C. 1 Potts, and Povey, whilst Messrs. Rhodes. Moore, and Wil- liamson cave valuable services. The executors of the late Mr. T. Jones, of South Bank Hotel, are the owners of the building, which had a fine outward appearance.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA-
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA-
TION. SELECTION OF CANDIDATE.

The annual meeting of the General Council of I this Association was held at the Club in Bewsey- street on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., president of the as- sociation, and amongst those also present were the Rev. E. Moore, Messrs. F. Monks, J.P.,Y. A. Roberts, W. Pierpoint, C. S. Burgess, Dr. Gomall, J.P., J. H. [Fleming. A. Browne, J. Walker, T. Birchall S. Bar- low, G. Plumpton, H. Roberts, sec., &c.

div.head: IGLECTION OF OFFICF.II9,
div.p: IGLECTION OF OFFICF.II9,

Mr. C. S. Sultanas proposed that Mr. 11cMinnies be re-elected president of the association. It was necessary, he thought, in times like those to have leaders in wilt:6 they had the most implicit confi- dence, and every member of the association would- know that Mr. McMinuies had been the trusted leader of the Liberal party in Warrington far forty years. Ile was sure that they would always be an- xious that lie should remain their leader.. (Cheers.) —Mr. DvABOBIGIN seconded the resolution, which, having been passed with cheers, was briefly ack- nowledged by Mr. MCMINNIES, who said that to the best of hie ability he would deserve the con- fidence of the association in the future.

Dr. GororAu. proposed that the vice-presidents of the association be Mr. George Crosfield; Mr.. John Crosfield, Alderman Burgess, and. Mr. F. Monks,. To Mr. George Crosfield and Mr. jobb. Crosfield the cause of Liberalism in Warrington wasi greatly in- debted, and the work. of Alderman Burgess in the same cause had been very great. Mr. Monks had also done valiant work in the past. He had great pleasure in proposing the election of the gentlemen I named. (Cheers.) Mr. Pt.usurrorr seconded the resolution.. He did not think, he remarked, that there was anyone who more valued the services of Mr. Monks- than, he did, and he well remembered that on the occasion when their esteemed president was returned mem- ber of Parliament for Warrington the way in which Mr. Monks worked. Mr- Monks' services had been very valuable. Mr. MONKS, in repin.thanked. the meeting.on,be- half of the whole of the gentlemen elected.. Mr. F. A. ROBERTS•proposed that Mr.W.Pierpoint be re-elected honorary treasurer.—Mr. T. BIRCHALL seconded the pro.position; which was carried; and Mr. PizePoiirr, in reply, intimated that it would give him great pleasure- to receive subscriptions. They must kee? Liberalism going ahead in War- rington. (Cheers.) SELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE., ,

• Mr. Winton said that he had great pleasure in proposing that Mr..john Crosfield—(cheers)—be the candidate at the next Parliamentary election for Warrington. They all knew Mr. Crosfield 's qualities as a candidate; and he was sure it was un- necessary for him to say anything in his favour. Be had great pleasure in proposing that Mr. Cros- • field be asked to be the Liberal candidate. (Cheers). —Mr. War.- BROAJAILTD.SE seconded the resolution, and. Mr. MONKS. also spoke. He referred to the dif- ferent views held by Liberals-as to the best mode of settling the Irish question,,and intimated that he should reserve the right. to take the course which , he thought best in the circumstances of the times. —Mr. Join-WALKER said that he saw signs that the Liberal party would soon be more united. In reading Mr. Chamberlain's-speech that day he was astonished to find that he (Mr. Chamberlain) inti- - mated that so far as the establishment of a Parliament for Ireland was 'concerned, he was not disposed to interfere with the wishes of the people of Ireland. That showed that he had come to the principle and to the practice,of Home Rule. He heartily supported the resolution, for.he felt sure that there was not a man in the Liberal party in Warrington, barring Mr. McMinnies,, who could rally the forces of Liberalism in Warrington, and cduld reach the heart of the people as well' as Mr. John Crosfield. (Cheers.) The Rev.. EDWARD Moons also supported' the motion. Speaking in, regard to Ireland, he said that, having tried the policy of force for all these weary years, the result was not such, in his jiidg-- ment, as to justify a continuance of that poliey, It appearedto him that if a patient had been harshly treated for years, and it had not agreed with him, the treatment should be changed. He felt sure that the policy to be pursued by England with' re-• gard'to the sister island was one of conciliation, of kindness, of generosity, and of justice, to which she had so long been a stringer. (Cheers.). There was no.other solution of the Irish difficulty than •a large and liberal measure of Home Rule for Ire- land. He had very much pleasure in supporting the candidature of Mr. Crosfield. He thought that perhaps of all men in Warrington he was the best candidate for the Liberal party. He hoped that the time was not far distant when Warrington would be able to • have a representative worthy of the name. (Cheers.)—Mr. J. SHAW GREEN, in a few words, also supported the motion. Mr. PruniPron intimated that he should bbth work and vote for Mr. Crosfitld, and Mt. S. BARLOW. in supporting the motion o said that he was delighted beyond measure with the address that Mr. Crosfield put before the electors 'at the last election. He be- lieved in "Honest John," who was the heart and soul of Liberalism in Warrington. (Cheers.)—Mr. Patoni- LEY- and Mr. L. &mum having spoken, the CHAIRMAN; said that in his opinion they could not have a better candidate than Mr. John Crosfield. (Cheers.)—The resolution haying been unanimously carried, a vote of thanks was passed to the chair- man, on the Motion af Mr. MONKS, seconded by Mr. FLEMING..

div.head: WARRIN.GTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRIN.GTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse • yesterday morning. _ There were present the Rev G P Roberts. presiding; and Mors W Long, Jolley, Greening, Derbyshire, J Houghton, Kitchell, Pennington, Gibson, W 'Houghton, Owen, Swinton' J Rylands, S Sutton (clerk), Dr Sephton (medical officer), W Owen (surveyor), and 7 Kerfoot (inspector.) THE SANKEL BEOOE.—The CLIME said he bad wri'len to the Town Clerk-of St. Helens and to the Clerk of the Presoot Union Rural Sanitary Authority with reference to the complaints about Sankey Brook. He bad received an acknowledgment from the Town Clerk of St. Helens, but he had beard nothing further from either St. Helens or the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority. Stravaron's ItErotar.—Mr. GWEN reported that plans were submitted by Mr. Tildesley for 15 houses in Welltield- street, Lovely-lane, which might be approved. Plans were also submitted by Messrs. Lever Bros. for three sheds partly within and partly without the borough, which, In his opin- ion, might be approved.—The report WRS adopted. MEDICAL 07FICER'8 REPORT.—Dr. SEPETGOI reported, for the month ending January 31st, that the births were, males 13, females 12, total 23; for deaths, males 13, females 16, total 29k The death rate from all causes was equal to 258 per 1,000, against 14 kthe average of the last three months. Since their last meeting he had inspeotod Massey and Norris Brooks, both of which he found in a far better condition than at his, last visit in Septembee 1835, although the suggestions he then made had not been acted upon. The reservoir at Mr. Deakin'o,tannery had been cleared out, which weuld considerably improve Norris Brook far some time, Still he thought the proprietors were not using every available or possible means to preserve the purity of the brook, and he would recommend the amtling tanks and filter beds to be casriea out as far as proposed in his report for September 1885:4, The brook, near Messrs. Pieepoint and Bryant's skin yard, at Latchford, be found polluted by lime water and the wasbing of skins. Ile made the same suggestion for thopreservance of this stream, as for Norris Brook. That ha found, had only partially bean carried out by settling tanks, bat no filter beds had been added. He would recommend that notice be served on ; Messrs. Pierpoiat and Bryant to, abate the pollution of the stream bv passing the waste water through filter beds be- fore turning it into ti,e brook. Ells attention had been directed to the pollution of a ditch by the Warrington Gas Committee. The ditch ras along the north side of the works from the railway to Winwiek-road, and was fouled by gas water, and toe drainage through an embankment made of chernio4 waste. A covered drain was required to be car- ried either into the sewer in Winwick-road or under the railway into the common receptacle for filth, namely Sankey Brook.—lt was agreed that the recommendation of the Medical Officer should be carried out in each case referred to in the above report. THE DEATH Or THE CHAlRmAN.—References were made to the death of the Chairinau of the Authority, Mr. C. Broadbent, a report of which will be found airing with other references to the event.—Afterwards Mr. DARIATsitIDE moyed that the vice-chairman, the Rey. G. F. Roberts be
appointed chairman until ths corry7lrtion thq fee which Mr. Broadbent had iy,.?en ap'pointed,—This prcpoti` was seconded by Mr. GBEENIWG, and agreed tu. This was all the business.

"I will engage that he will not expect you, if you will only promise me:' "On that condition I will not meet him; that is, if you will give me a token." , , . "Name one yourself.", "Give me your darling hand to kiss." Presently her Voice was heard to say, "Now I am just going to open the door a wee bit. Are you ready ?" . "Yes, dear Marie." . "Very well; now—be quick." • Simultaneously the door opened slightlyeandthe sound of a long lovingekiss was heard in the gloom. "There, Achille, that will do. Are you satisfied now "0 Marie, my own my very own! never, 0 never, shall I forget the touch of your darling hand !" "Now, Achille, you must really go. Good-night." "Good night, my beloved." Then the door cloied, and silence reigned again in the corridor. An attentive listener, however, at Marie de Lisle's door might have heard for a good half-hour suc- cessive peals'of laughter, in which a couple of voices were distinctly recognisable. Mlle. de Lisle did net appear that morning at the table d'hote, and both Captain Morgan and Madame de Lisle were absent also. The Colonel, at the sight of the vacant chairs, was considerably surprised and most un- easy. Nor was his equanimity restored on learning that the whole party had gone to London. To follow them, he felt, would be undignified in the extreme. But there was nothing to prevent his writing to beg -Marie to return, and promising himself the plea- sure of slashing the Captain across the face at sight. To his cousin he wrote thus r— "My dear Nlarie,—Your conduct is inexplicable. Only a few hours ago you promised solemnly, to think seriously of marrying me, and now I find ;you have left, suddenly for England, in the company of Captain Morgan. If you are not mad, you will ,return here at once, before the news of your escapade gets to the ears of uncle George. Once more I warn you that the consequences of your folly would be, should he hear it, most serious for you. 0 Marie, be wise! By the darling hand which but a few hours ago you gave as a token of good faith to my loving lips, I implore yeu to return to your ever forgiv- ing and adoring / ACHILLE." "P.B.—You may tell your friend the Captain that I shall take the earliest opportunity of calling him to ac- count for his part in this proceeding." To this the lady replied "Dear Achille,—My conduct will not, I think, appear inexplicable when linform you that I am .now Mrs. Morgan, having been married with my mother's consent, and, for reasons of my own, privately, just a week ago. Should 'you fancy yourself aggrieved by what you may choose to consider a breach of faith, remember that all I engaged to do was • seriously to think of marrying you —some day when circumstances would permit,' and this I will certainly dcw at the proper time. Just at present, however, lam not a widow. With regard to me- expec- tations from poor dear uncle George, do not, I beg of you, make yourself uneasy about me on that score. The fact is, my mother received a telegram from Guadalotepe a fortnight ago announcing his death, aa well as giving the terms of his will, which were to the effect that his money should be divided, subject to no conditions, be- tween us equally. This is only right and fair, just as I always expected. I have given your message to Herbert. —Yours affectionately, MARIE. From Captain-Morgan to M. le Colonel Achille Leroy: "Sir,—ln reply to your message, I beg to inform you that I am at your orders whenever and wherever, abroad; you may desire to meet me. I would only add the re- quest that you will be pleased to be patient until the termination of our honeymoon, which we have arranged to spend in England. Ono word, in conclusion, of ad- vice. When next you are disposed for nocturnal amorous adventures, carry a light rith you, otherwise you may again mistake the foot of your rival for the hand of your darling.—Your obedient liervant, HERBERT Moscow."

WRECK OF A PASSENGER SHIP. NEW YORK, TOURSDAY.—A large passenger steamer, name unknown, is on the rocks off Monmouth Beach, on the New Jersey coast. The life-saving crew have left for the spot. The screams of the women are audible to the spectators on shore. A heavy sea is running, and there is some fog. THE WAR ALARMS. A farther heavy fall took place on the London Stock Ex- change in foreign securities an Thursday morning on re- newed sales on Continental account, and prices in the de- partment went down 1 to 3 per cent. PERTH. TIIIIRSDAY.—A decree prohibiting the export of horses frem Austria-Hungary is expected to be issued with- in the next few days. THE FIGHTING AT MASSOWAH. Penis, TEURSDAY.—The " Republique Francais° " to- day publishes a despatch from Suez, giving particulars of the disaster to the Italian troops near Massowah. The des- patch states that out of a total of 480 men enly 50 escaped, and that all the grins were captured by the Abvesinians. The Italians subsequently evacuated all their advanced positions, and the Abyssinians, on the 27th ult., attacked Massowah and forced the first line of entrenchments. It was considered doubtful whether the Italians would be able to hold out until the arrival of reinforcements.
